overall tensile behavior. Leech et al. [22], presented a more complex
quasi-static analysis of fibre ropes and included it in a commercial
software: fibre rope modeller (FRM). Their analysis is based on the prin-
ciple of virtual work and can take frictional effects into account. The
program expresses tension and torque as functions of elongation and
twist. Leech’s model appears to be very sophisticated, with an accurate
mechanical modeling of the components of the fibre ropes behavior
and their interactions. However, only axial and torsional actions are
taken into account. Kumar et al. [23] extended Costello’s model to
obtain analytical expressions for maximum contact stresses induced
in the strands with a metallic core. Huang [24] studied the contact
mode conditions for a seven wire strand. Jolicoeur [25] compared the
results obtained by several mathematical models of a seven wire strand,
specifically chosen with a geometry to explain the different contact
modes. The literature on the effects of interfacial contacts is limited.
Although a few studies have addressed the effects of friction at the
interfaces, the results show significant dispersion, since the parame-
ters considered vary from author to author. The effects of tangential
distributed forces at the contact surfaces are seldom considered. These
forces cause the wires to slip on the core and hence can change the
individual wire as well as the overall strand response. A mathematical
model to represent the effects of tangential and normal distributed
forces in a coupled contact was formulated by Parthasarathy [26].
Gnanavel et al. [27] presented an analytical model explaining the
importance of the interfacial loads and their effects in coupled contact.
They identified the threshold limit at which the contact mode changes
from a coupled arrangement to the arrangement of core-wire contact.
Ghoreishi et al. [28] developed a nonlinear elastic continuum model
for the analysis of the overall axial stiffness of fibrous structures with
a large number of twisted components. By contrast with multilayered
approaches, the structure under consideration is herein depicted as a
set of coaxial helices only characterized by their external lay angle and
corresponding radius. The contact and friction forces are neglected thus
no consideration about the energy dissipation is present in their work.
Gnanavel and Parthasarathy [29] presented a mathematical model for
the static behavior of a seven wire strand subjected to an axial tensile
load and twisting action. The mathematical model takes into account
the Poisson-effect in the wires, inter-wire pressure and the effects of
friction between the core and the helical wires to the strand stiffness
coefficients. Sauter and Hagedorn [30] employed distributed Jenkin
elements to model the damper cable of a Stockbridge damper [31].
The damper impedances was simulated using data obtained from a
simple experiment carried out with a piece of damper cable. In this
study the Masing model has been generalized for a continuous system
such as a cable. Gerges [32] conducted an experimental study dealing
with wire rope springs deforming in the tension-compression mode.
The authors developed a semi-analytical model that depends entirely
on the dimensions and properties of the springs. This model describes
the restoring force as a function of the displacement and the velocity
sign only. The restoring force was modeled as a direct summation of
two components: an elastic force and a damping force. The nonlinear
non-hysteretic elastic force was based on an equivalent cross-section
having the same area and moment of inertia of the wire rope. The large
displacement analysis was carried out using a consistent curved beam
element. The nonlinear hysteretic damping force was modeled as a

constants were empirically related to the dimensions of the springs.
The model agreed well with the experimental results. Sun et al. [33]
developed an elasto-plastic 3D contact problem of a strand using FE
analysis. In this work the augmented Lagrangian multiplier method has
been used to handle friction conditions between the centre wire and the
helical wire. The analyses were carried out by assigning displacements
as boundary conditions and, despite the constant forces are described
accurately, no hysteresis curves are presented. Ma et al. [34] developed
a model for several types of wire ropes with metal cores and built a geo-
metric model for the 6 × 19 IWS wire rope. A 3D finite element model
for calculating the deformation of wire rope was set up. Completely
constraining one end of the wire rope and applying an axial force to the
other, the authors numerically simulated the stresses and deformations
of the wire, obtaining the deformation distribution of each wire within
the wire rope under different laying directions. However no friction was
taken into account, hence, hysteresis curves are not discussed. Another
3D finite element approach, which considers friction and geometric
nonlinearities, is described in [35], where the hysteretic behavior of
a short steel strand subjected to coupled tensile-bending cycles was
obtained. However, the authors highlighted the computational burden
and noted that while the model provided a good qualitative description,
it fell short in providing a quantitative match with experimental results.

blocks.text:
The Kirchhoff–Love theory [16] for thin curvilinear beams is often
used as a basic model to study the mechanical behavior of wire ropes
subjected to tension and torsion. This approach allows to evaluate the
stress state in each wire and to predict the general behavior of the
rope. However, the stress state of the wires is derived with simplifying
assumptions about internal forces distribution, often using differential
equations of motion for curved beams thus ignoring the real distri-
bution of contact regions, which are generally discrete. The following
approaches explicitly account for the superhelix (doubly-twisted helix)
configuration of independent wires for multi-stranded ropes. Elata
et al. [36] set two limit kinematic hypotheses that emulate a well
lubricated rope and infinite friction between adjacent wires equivalent
to what is now termed as ‘full slip’ and ‘perfect stick’ states. Comparison
with experimental data in terms of stiffnesses showed general agree-
ment with the model’s predictions, even though the coefficients are
somewhat higher than those measured experimentally. Usabiaga and
Pagalday [37] set a new wire kinematics based again on the assumption
that friction between wires is high enough to prevent wire-sliding be-
tween adjacent wires in the strands, while Xiang et al. [38] developed
the model under the assumption of absence of friction between the
wires. Fraldi et al. [39] investigated the tension-torsion strength and
stiffness of helically arranged bundles, observing that the different cross
sections and helical angles of the layers determine a non-homogeneous
stress redistribution when one or more wires break.

With the aim of exploiting the dissipative capabilities of wire ropes,
the bending problem of the strand is also addressed in the literature.
When a strand is bent, internal frictional forces arise and initially tend
to counteract the relative sliding of the strands. When a limit deflection
is reached, these forces are overcome by the difference in normal forces
between adjacent wires, and this causes relative sliding. As already
mentioned, this phenomenon constitutes a dissipative mechanism ex-
ploited in applications and gives rise to the experimentally observable
hysteretic behavior of ropes subjected to bending. Concerning the
bending behavior, a first major contribution is the work of Papail-
iou [40], who developed a mechanical model for strands subjected to
simultaneous tensile and bending loads and obtains the maximum and
minimum stiffnesses.

However, as noted by the authors themselves, the maximum stiffness

for estimating the yield curvature of ropes subjected to bending and

providing estimates of the dissipation and self-damping.

Carboni et al. [46,47] employed a phenomenological approach in
which they generalized the Bouc-Wen model to identify the hysteresis
cycles exhibited by short wire ropes made of steel and NiTiNOL under
coupled tension-bending loadings. These models provide an accurate
description of hysteretic softening and hardening behaviors resulting
from the interaction of geometric, frictional and material nonlinearities,
and they can be suitably applied for both static and dynamic prob-
lems [48,49]. However, according to the phenomenological nature, a
direct correlation with the mechanical and geometrical properties of
the wire ropes is not established. Furthermore, Carboni et al. [50]
proposed a semi-phenomenological model consisting of a planar shear-
deformable beam equipped with material and geometric nonlinearities.
Specifically, a Bouc-Wen relationship between bending moment and
curvature was implemented to capture the loading-unloading hysteresis
cycles, while a fraction of the circular area that encloses the wire ropes’
section was assumed to estimate the elastic stiffness.

The present work, taking inspiration from previous achievements,
proposes a mechanical model providing robust estimates of the maxi-
mum and minimum stiffness for short ropes in bending as well as under
axial-torsional loading. For the purposes of this research, a short rope is
defined as a rope element, having a ratio of cross-sectional diameter to
length between 1∕12 and 1∕5, whose bending stiffness dominates the
mechanical response in terms of bending moments and shear forces.
One of the novelties of the model is the capability of handling multi-
strands as well as simple-strand ropes. The elastic problem for the beam
is solved analytically and the explicit expressions for the displacements
are given in terms of the beam stiffness matrix coefficients. The elastic-
ity matrix for the beam is obtained starting from the internal structure
and the geometric and material properties of single wires.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 illustrates the mechan-
ical model developed for interpreting the structural response of wire
ropes in the linear regime. Section 3 presents the experimental setup
and post-processing of the results in terms of maximum and minimum
stiffness attained in the hysteresis cycles by short ropes subjected to
pure bending. Finally, Section 4 and Section 5 illustrate the analytical
solutions of the boundary value problems and the comparisons of
the theoretical maximum and minimum stiffnesses with experimental
results for the bending tests performed and for the axial-torsional tests
available in the literature, respectively.

blocks.text:
Wire ropes are artifacts that, when subjected to suitable loading con-
ditions, undergo geometric rearrangements of the internal structure due
to the relative sliding between individual wires. The formulation of a
continuum model that can properly describe the prevailing mechanical
response should account for this essential feature. In the here proposed
model, this aspect is accounted for by the introduction of eigenstrains
affecting the constitutive response of individual wires, as shown below.

This case, which is referred to in the literature as the ‘stick state’
(see e.g. [52]), shows the classical beam kinematics and it is expected
to describe well the maximum stiffness attainable by the rope, under
the assumptions that no relative inter-wire sliding occurs. However,
it is found that this assumption leads to an overestimation of the
rope’s maximum stiffness which is an order of magnitude greater than
the experimental one (as shown in the next sections and as already
observed in [53]). A possible explanation is that the magnitude of
the deformations under pure bending for which the rope behaves as a
monolithic beam (i.e., perfect stick state) is so small that it becomes
hard to see it experimentally. From a phenomenological standpoint,
it is observed that the wires within the cable always undergo relative
sliding, resulting in a kinematic model that, at the macroscopic level,
is not compatible with that of a standard beam. As the deformations
increase, the rope undergoes a change of reference configuration af-
fecting the wires’ constitutive response. This feature can be effectively
described making use of the concept of eigenstrain, (see, e.g., [54]) that
is widely exploited in studying dislocations, point defects in solids and
other structural changes as well as by Eshelby in developing his well-
known theory of inclusions [55]. In the linearized regime, the total
compatible strain in the beam is given by the sum of the elastic part
and the eigenstrain, both of which may be kinematically incompatible.

same stick–slip state. Breaking the symmetry in the wires’ stick–slip
states would lead to the emergence of different stiffness matrix coeffi-
cients with values depending on the position along the rope centerline.
Despite this model opens up the possibility for more detailed analyses,
in this work it is only shown how the aforementioned limit hypotheses
lead to sufficiently accurate predictions of the maximum and minimum
stiffnesses in agreement with experimental measurements.

lines.text: Some remarks about Eq. (18) are necessary to put this more clearly
in the context of the ensuing wire rope model. Firstly, in addition to the
well-known coupling between axial and torsional behavior, a coupling
between shearing and bending behavior is also observed in the present
model. Furthermore, in general, 𝑘𝑖𝑗≠𝑘𝑗 𝑖for 𝑖≠𝑗except for the
perfect stick state and thus the stiffness matrix obtained in this way
is always positive definite but not symmetric except for perfect stick
(which happens to be the case of classical beam theory). As a matter of
a fact, the values of the stiffness matrix coefficients 𝑘11, 𝑘22, 𝑘33, 𝑘41, 𝑘52
and 𝑘63 are the same for all states while 𝑘14, 𝑘25, 𝑘36, 𝑘44, 𝑘55 and 𝑘66
attain different values since the eigenstrains affect the way in which the
wire rope curvatures govern the wires’ strains. Another remark is that
the constitutive matrix in Eq. (18) is independent of the coordinate 𝑠
and preserves the given structure only when all wires belong to the
same stick–slip state. Breaking the symmetry in the wires’ stick–slip
states would lead to the emergence of different stiffness matrix coeffi-
cients with values depending on the position along the rope centerline.
Despite this model opens up the possibility for more detailed analyses,
in this work it is only shown how the aforementioned limit hypotheses
lead to sufficiently accurate predictions of the maximum and minimum
stiffnesses in agreement with experimental measurements.

blocks.text: 3. Experimental tests on short wire-ropes subjected to bending

lines.text: 3. Experimental tests on short wire-ropes subjected to bending

blocks.text:
A quasi-static experimental campaign was performed to collect a set
of representative results to be used for the validation of the model. A
single-strand and a multi-strand wire rope, with cross-sections shown
in Fig. 2, were tested by making use of the universal material testing
machine MTS 810 equipped with a custom-made setup, shown in Fig. 3.
The single-strand rope, henceforth denoted by R1, has an average
diameter of 2 cm, while the seven-strands rope, referred to as R2, has
an average diameter of 1 cm.

blocks.text:
The target of the experimental tests was the acquisition of the
hysteresis cycles of short wire ropes subjected to pure bending loading
programs. The setup comprised two rigid arms, each one equipped with
two clamps for constraining the ropes’ ends. The clamps were realized
with two steel plates having cylindrical housings to host the ropes
tightened by four bolts. The left arm was rigidly connected to a steel
top plate that, in turn, was anchored to the load cell of the MTS 810.
The right arm was connected to a bottom steel plate fixed to the moving
piston of the testing machine. Fig. 3(a) and (b) show a couple of tested
wire ropes in the reference and deformed configuration, respectively.
In the former, the wire ropes are stress free while, in the latter, they
are subjected to flexural deformation due to upward or downward
movement of the right arm. In order to avoid hardening effects due to
tensile forces in the ropes, a horizontal slider was placed between the
right arm and the bottom steel plate so that the displaced rope ends can
freely approach the left ends. In this configuration, when the right rope
ends are displaced, the load cell connected to the left arm measures the
total restoring force due to the internal shear forces in the ropes.

blocks.text: 4.2. R2 stranded rope analysis

lines.text: 4.2. R2 stranded rope analysis

blocks.text:
The R2 rope shown in Fig. 2(b) has a layout of 1 + 6 strands with
each strand having 1 + 6 + 12 wires. The pitches have been measured
directly on the sample as shown in Fig. 10. With the usual pitch sign
convention, the geometrical features are reported in Tables 4 and 5. The
wires are made of AISI 304 steel, having Young’s modulus 𝐸= 200 GPa
and Poisson’s ratio 𝜈= 0.3. Fig. 11 shows the maximum and minimum
stiffnesses as function of the R2 rope length according to the proposed
model and the experimental results. As for the single-strand rope, the
full slip and the partial stick states deliver a good prediction of the
minimum and maximum stiffness, respectively. The larger differences
between the proposed formulation and the experiments are obtained for
the lowest length of 5 cm. In this case, the model is not completely rep-
resentative of the sample response where the boundary effects become
relevant because the pitch of the lateral strand is larger than the total
length of the rope. This fact became apparent during the experiments
carried out for this short length, where the torsional effects became
clear.

blocks.text: 6. Conclusions

lines.text: 6. Conclusions

blocks.text:
This paper addressed the problem of modeling the mechanical
response of metallic wire ropes aiming at providing robust estimates of
the stiffnesses associated with different regimes, from perfect interwire
stick to full slip.

lines.text: This paper addressed the problem of modeling the mechanical
response of metallic wire ropes aiming at providing robust estimates of
the stiffnesses associated with different regimes, from perfect interwire
stick to full slip.

blocks.text:
A new mechanical model employing linear constitutive relation-
ships was presented and proven to accurately predict the upper and
lower bounds of the stiffness which were experimentally measured. The
wire rope is modeled as a classical shear-deformable Timoshenko beam
in the linear regime and the constitutive equations are derived taking
into account accurate wires’ geometry and material properties.

lines.text: A new mechanical model employing linear constitutive relation-
ships was presented and proven to accurately predict the upper and
lower bounds of the stiffness which were experimentally measured. The
wire rope is modeled as a classical shear-deformable Timoshenko beam
in the linear regime and the constitutive equations are derived taking
into account accurate wires’ geometry and material properties.

blocks.text:
An incompatible eigenstrain term was introduced in the wires’
strain measures to account for the inter-slip between adjacent wires.
The eigenstrains assume different expressions according to the rope’s
strain regime and are assumed to depend linearly on the rope strains.
Specifically, three interwire stick–slip conditions were identified for the

The eigenstrains assume different expressions according to the rope’s
strain regime and are assumed to depend linearly on the rope strains.
Specifically, three interwire stick–slip conditions were identified for the

blocks.text:

the full slip state.

blocks.text:
The wire’s constitutive relationships were obtained by extending
Saint-Venant’s theory to curvilinear rods, and the overall rope’s con-
stitutive relations were accordingly obtained. The model is charac-
terized by a generally non-symmetric positive-definite stiffness matrix
exhibiting coupling between bending and shear besides the well-known
coupling between axial and torsional problems.

lines.text: The wire’s constitutive relationships were obtained by extending
Saint-Venant’s theory to curvilinear rods, and the overall rope’s con-
stitutive relations were accordingly obtained. The model is charac-
terized by a generally non-symmetric positive-definite stiffness matrix
exhibiting coupling between bending and shear besides the well-known
coupling between axial and torsional problems.

blocks.text:
An experimental campaign was carried out on single- and multi-
strand short wire ropes subjected to pure bending making use of a
tailored experimental apparatus. The experiments were carried out by
subjecting the ropes to quasi-static end displacements by means of a
low frequency input. The results obtained from the experimental tests
in terms of force–displacement cycles at the rope ends were employed
to extract the maximum and minimum stiffness attained across the
hysteresis cycles through a linear regression.

lines.text: An experimental campaign was carried out on single- and multi-
strand short wire ropes subjected to pure bending making use of a
tailored experimental apparatus. The experiments were carried out by
subjecting the ropes to quasi-static end displacements by means of a
low frequency input. The results obtained from the experimental tests
in terms of force–displacement cycles at the rope ends were employed
to extract the maximum and minimum stiffness attained across the
hysteresis cycles through a linear regression.

blocks.text:
With the present model, the boundary-value problem for the rope
under end displacements could be solved analytically for the cases
examined and the displacements were provided in dimensionless form
together with the explicit expression of the stiffness. The model’s
predictions were compared with the experimental results obtained for
the two ropes tested under bending, showing a good agreement in
both the lower and upper bounds of the stiffness. The theoretical
predictions were also compared with the experimental results available
in the literature concerning single-strand wire ropes subjected to axial-
torsional tests, showing a good agreement. A remarkable feature of this
model is that no calibration of any physical parameter is required to
accurately estimate the magnitude of the limit stiffnesses.

lines.text: With the present model, the boundary-value problem for the rope
under end displacements could be solved analytically for the cases
examined and the displacements were provided in dimensionless form
together with the explicit expression of the stiffness. The model’s
predictions were compared with the experimental results obtained for
the two ropes tested under bending, showing a good agreement in
both the lower and upper bounds of the stiffness. The theoretical
predictions were also compared with the experimental results available
in the literature concerning single-strand wire ropes subjected to axial-
torsional tests, showing a good agreement. A remarkable feature of this
model is that no calibration of any physical parameter is required to
accurately estimate the magnitude of the limit stiffnesses.

blocks.text:
The present linear model provides sufficiently accurate estimates of
the upper/lower stiffnesses. However, the prediction of the hysteresis
cycle or the response under bending and tension still requires further
efforts.

blocks.text:
ABSTRACT
In this paper, based on three-dimensional phenomenological model and using a user-defined
material subroutine mechanical behavior of shape memory alloy (SMA) wire ropes (or cables) and
their components have been studied through implicit solution method in Abaqus software.
Material parameters have been extracted using available experimental data and numerical simula-
tions. Due to the convoluted geometry and interwire contact status within a cable, a finite elem-
ent analysis is firstly performed for a 1  37 steel wire rope to validate modeling and mechanical
interactions of a wire rope. Afterwards, superelastic and shape memory effect cables with different
constructions (7 7 and 1  27) are studied and their mechanical behavior including normal stress,
shear stress, strain, and temperature diagrams as well as the relationship between axial force and
displacement for a full cable and each component are extracted. Furthermore, the SMA wire ropes
have been optimized in terms of achieving maximum specific energy through experimental design
method. Comparison of numerical results with experimental data indicates the acceptable
accuracy of this study.

blocks.text:
becomes permanently deformed (bird cage phenomenon)
[2]. In order to incur such defects and improve the perform-
ance of wire ropes, the use of shape memory alloy (SMA)
cables has widely received a great attention. Due to their
unique characteristics including superelasticity, shape mem-
ory effect, high energy absorption, adequate tensile strength,
high corrosion resistance, and the ability to recover large
strains, these cables are resistant to twisting and impact
loads [7]. In contrast to other conventional cables, SMA
wire ropes owing to their high energy density, can provide a
design with the higher power but the lower volume [1, 7].
Shape memory effect structures (SME) can be act as a ther-
mal lock or thermal actuator due to the detwinning process
[8–15]. Large-load capacity and high impact energy absorp-
tion can be considered as an inherit characterization of these
cables [1]. The use of superelastic (SE) cables may be also
common in dentistry [7], relieving congestion [16], cellular
phone antenna [17], and vibration alleviation of earthquakes
[18]. Several researches explore mechanical properties of SE
wire ropes [19–23]. An analytical, numerical and experimen-
tal study of SE coil spring under axial loading is performed
using three-dimensional model [19]. Mechanical response of
a set of SE wire ropes with two constructions of 7  7 and
1  27 under tensile stress is investigated experimentally [1,
7]. Mas et al. [20] explored the performance of Ni-Ti SMA

Considering the above efforts, a detail study on the
behavior of SME cables has received less attention. The
main motivation of this paper is to explore the mechanical
properties of SMA cables with 1  27 and 7  7 construc-
tions and their components for both SME as well as SE fea-
tures. Furthermore, SMA cable is optimized with the aim of
accomplishing maximum specific energy. Among proposed
SMA phenomenological models [31–38], we employ the one
known as Souza model owing to its simplicity and appropri-
ate agreements with the experimental data. To simulate
material properties of SMA cables, this model has been
implemented through UMAT subroutine in Abaqus envir-
onment. Comparing finite element analysis (FEA) of 1  37
steel cable with the available numerical results [5] confirms
the veracity of modeling as well as mechanical interactions
between wires and strands. We also investigate mechanical
behavior of SE cables with the 7  7 and 1  27 construc-
tions, and then their components for normal stress-strain-
temperature and shear stress-strain-temperature diagrams
are extracted. Optimization of SMA wire ropes is also car-
ried out to achieve the maximum specific energy using the
design of experiment method [36].

characteristics of lay, texture, and pitch (or lay length) defining
as the direction of wires and/or strands wrapped around core,
the state of wires placement within a strand, and distance of a
single revolution around core, respectively. Based on the cross

blocks.text: 4. Simulation of steel and SMA wire ropes

lines.text: 4. Simulation of steel and SMA wire ropes

blocks.text:
In this section, to validate the process of modeling and
interwire contact status, a steel cable with cross section of
1  37 in the elastic range is analyzed using finite element
method and then we simulate the SE wire ropes for both
single-helix 1  27, and double-helix 7  7 configurations.
The results of steel and SE cables are compared with avail-
able numerical [5] and experimental data [7]. Based on this
validation, the SMA wire rope under SME feature is studied,
and both single- and double-helix cables are modeled, and
their mechanical behavior are simulated in detail for the first
time. In this FEA, the implicit solution method may be
employed; however, this method seems complex and time-
consumer comparing with explicit solution, it offers more
accuracy of the results in dynamic mode.

blocks.text:
obtained through FEA and then compared with experimen-
tal data. Furthermore, single- and double-helix SME cables
are simulated and the relationship between of both normal
and shear stresses with strain and temperature variation
along with force-displacement diagrams for components are
investigated. Moreover, optimization of the 1  27 SME
cable to fulfill the maximum specific energy is carried out in
terms of two controllable variables including wire diameter
and helix angle and then the optimized corresponding val-
ues are suggested. The force-displacement and normal
stress-strain diagrams show that although the axial force in
core wires seems to be relatively insignificant, due to small
cross-sectional area these wires have always the largest nor-
mal stress. From inner layers to outers, the normal stress
starts decreasing while the axial force does not follow a spe-
cific trend so that for different elongations different cable
components could have the highest axial force. In the shear
stress-strain-temperature diagram of SME cables, lays of
individual components contribute to positive and/or nega-
tive sign of shear stress. Finally, upon heating these cables,
they recover inelastic strains in very short range of time and
specific range of temperature. The results of optimization
also shows that the more wire diameter and the less helix
angle can lead to the greater specific energy of a wire rope.

blocks.text: A B S T R A C T

lines.text: A B S T R A C T

blocks.text:
NiTi alloys exhibit high damping capacity and superelasticity. However, their internal friction peak typically 
occurs near the martensitic transformation temperature, limiting their applications over a wide temperature 
window as damping devices. Herein, with NiTi microfilaments introducing sequential localized phase trans­
formations, structural deformation and inter-wire friction dissipation, the periodic braided microfilament 
transformed the internal friction peak into a high broad damping plateau with a reduced modulus. Notably, the 
88B microfilament exhibited a high tanδ (~0.11) and low storage modulus (~3.6 GPa) across a wide temper­
ature window exceeding 145 ◦C. This work realizes the synergistic optimization of high damping, ultra-low 
stiffness, and temperature insensitivity in NiTi wires, offering a promising strategy for designing high- 
performance damping devices under complex environments.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

lines.text: 1. Introduction

blocks.text:
NiTi shape memory alloys are widely utilized in aerospace and pre­
cision instruments due to their high damping capacity,[1–3] which pri­
marily originates from reversible martensitic transformation (MT) and 
the motion of abundant movable twin boundaries.[4,5] However, the 
damping peak is typically restricted to a narrow transformation tem­
perature range, exhibiting temperature dependence.[6] In the fully 
austenitic or martensitic phase, the absence of mobile phase interfaces 
reduces damping capacity, with a substantial contrast in loss tangent 
(tanδ) between the two phases.[7] To broaden damping performance in a 
wide temperature window, reduce temperature sensitivity, and improve 
modulus stability, second phases have been introduced to induce local 
transformation stress fields.[8] Alternatively, structural designs such as 
porous NiTi and bicontinuous interpenetrating Mg-NiTi composites can 
simultaneously enhance strength and damping capacity.[9] In this study, 
we developed novel NiTi braided microfilaments featuring a spatial 
helical architecture to achieve enhanced wide-temperature damping 
and a tunable elastic modulus. The spatial interlacing and bending of 
wires in the braided architecture create spring-like mechanical units that

helical architecture to achieve enhanced wide-temperature damping
and a tunable elastic modulus. The spatial interlacing and bending of
wires in the braided architecture create spring-like mechanical units that

blocks.text: 2. Experimental

lines.text: 2. Experimental

blocks.text:
The material information and braiding process details have been 
described in detail in our previous paper.[10] Single-braided microfila­
ments were fabricated using 4, 8, and 12 NiTi wires on a high-speed 
braiding machine, denoted as 4B, 8B, and 12B, respectively, with a 
braiding density parameter (picks per inch, ppi) set to 50. Double- 
braided microfilaments (denoted as 88B) were prepared by re-braiding 
eight 8B microfilaments using an identical manufacturing process. 8 
wires were also prepared with ppi values of 25 and 80, denoted as ppi25 
and ppi80, respectively. The damping capacity and storage modulus 
were studied with a TA Q850 dynamic mechanical analyzer (DMA) at a 
fixed strain amplitude of 20 μm at different frequencies and a cooling 
and heating rate of 5 ◦C/min. The tests were performed over a broad 
temperature window ranging from −70 ◦C to 75 ◦C.

Fig. 2a and b exhibit morphologies of 8B-NiTi and 88B-NiTi micro­
filaments. In contrast to the single wire (Fig. 1), the storage modulus 
decreases significantly after single braiding (Fig. 2d) and further de­
creases following the double-braid process (Fig. 2e). Specifically, the 
storage modulus of 8B-NiTi is at approximately 11 GPa during cooling 
process and 12 GPa during heating process, which further decreases to 
~3.6 GPa and ~4.3 GPa in 88B-NiTi. Furthermore, over the tested 
temperature range of 145 ◦C, the tanδ of the braided microfilaments 
remains temperature-insensitive, transitioning into a high broad inter­
nal friction plateau that demonstrates superior thermomechanical sta­
bility. Throughout the temperature range, the tanδ of 8B-NiTi remains 
stable at 0.02–0.05, exhibiting a significantly improved damping ca­
pacity in the austenite phase compared with the single wire. Notably, 
Fig. 2f demonstrates that the tanδ curves of 8B are nearly identical after 
10 thermal cycles, evidencing the excellent cycling stability of the 
damping mechanism. Cyclic tensile tests were further conducted on 
braided microfilaments, as shown in Fig. S1. Upon further double- 
braiding process, the 88B microfilaments achieve a higher tanδ of 
0.06–0.11 over a wide temperature window. Notably, the tanδ and 
modulus curves at 1 Hz and 5 Hz nearly overlap, revealing excellent 
frequency stability and reliable damping under variable conditions. 
Moreover，we compared the damping capacity of stainless steel wire, 
stainless steel braided microfilament, and twisted stainless steel wire, as 
shown in Fig. S2.

Within 8B, individual NiTi wires follow a helical path (Fig. 2c), 
forming a continuous micro-spring network that converts structural 
deformation into localized bending and torsion. This inhomogeneous 
stress distribution within braided structure induces sequential localized 
MT,[10] broadening the intrinsic damping peak into a wide plateau. 88B 
microfilament creates a micro-spring network that dissipates vibration 
energy progressively from outer to inner architectures,[11] further 
enhancing damping performance. Simultaneously, abundant contact 
sites generate micro-sliding friction interfaces, enabling efficient energy 
dissipation.

As shown in Fig. 3a and b, increasing the number of wires increases 
the density of inter-wire contact sites. The tanδ of 4B is smooth and 
maintains a lower value of 0.008–0.02 (Fig. 3c), and 12B achieves a 
higher tanδ value of 0.03–0.06 (Fig. 3d). With the ppi maintained at 50, 
all samples (4B, 8B and 12B) show a broad damping plateau without 
distinct internal friction peaks. Overall, damping capacity improves 
with the increasing number of wires. The storage modulus of 4B remains 
around 17–19 GPa, and 12B reaches approximately 18–22 GPa. As the 
wire increases from 4B to 8B and 12B, exhibits no distinct abrupt 
change, displaying temperature independence. Increasing the wire 
count raises the wire volume fraction, synchronously increasing the 
interwoven micro-springs and contact sites, thereby simultaneously 
enhancing structural damping and frictional dissipation via micro- 
sliding.

blocks.text: 4. Conclusion

lines.text: 4. Conclusion

blocks.text:
In summary, braided NiTi microfilaments couple intrinsic MT with 
structural energy dissipation to achieve a flat damping plateau and 
reduced stiffness over a wide temperature window (>145 ◦C). Spatial 
constraints introduce inhomogeneity stress, enabling a sequential MT 
that converts the damping peak of a single wire into a high-damping 
plateau. Braided wires act as micro-springs that transform vibration 
into individual wire bending and torsional strains, driving inter-wire 
micro-sliding friction. From single to double braiding, modulus de­
creases while damping improves. Increasing wire count improves 
damping capacity, whereas increasing ppi reduces both damping ca­
pacity and storage modulus. Braided microfilaments overcome the 
narrow damping window and high modulus of conventional NiTi wires, 
providing a strategy for high-performance damping devices in complex 
thermomechanical environments.

blocks.text:
With high flexibility and slim body, flexible robots have been widely used in minimally invasive
surgery because they can safely reach the lesion deep inside the human body through small incisions
or natural orifices. However, high stiffness of robot body is also required for transferring force and
maintaining the motion accuracy. To meet these two contradictory requirements, various methods
have been implemented to enable adjustable stiffness for flexible surgical robots. In this review, we first
summarize the anatomic constraints of common natural tracts of human body to provide a guidance
for the design of variable stiffness flexible robots. And then, the variable stiffness methods have been
categorized based on their basic principles of varying the stiffness. In the end, two variable stiffness
methods with great potential and the moving strategy of variable stiffness flexible robots are discussed.

blocks.text: 1.1. Flexible surgical robots in minimally invasive surgery

lines.text: 1.1. Flexible surgical robots in minimally invasive surgery

blocks.text:
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) includes single or multi-
port surgery and natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery
(NOTES), as shown in Fig. 1. MIS offers advantages such as de-
creasing the pain of the patient, reducing the recovery time,
enhancing the safety of the surgery, etc. Therefore, it has be-
come prevalent in past decades, and robot-assisted MIS has also
developed rapidly [1,2].

developed rapidly [1,2].

blocks.text:
The surgical instruments are required to have a dexterous and
slender body, which allows them to access the lesion deep inside
the human body and carry out surgeries during MIS. Therefore,
flexible robots with small outer diameter and plenty of degrees
of freedom for maneuverability are used widely in MIS [3].

the human body, resulting in low working accuracy and stability
of the robot. And low stiffness also limits the robots’ performance

Many variable stiffness mechanisms have been applied on large-
scale robots to change performance. For example, prostheses en-
hance their adaptability in different working scenarios by equip-
ping with spring-based variable stiffness mechanisms [19], robot
maintains precise force sensing ability by real-time controlling
the joint motor [20], continuum robot output programmable force
by using pneumatic based variable stiffness outer sheath [21], etc.

blocks.text:
However, since flexible robots are constructed with consecu-
tive joints or continuum elastomers, which featuring slim bod-
ies and small cross sections, common variable stiffness mecha-
nisms with large scales cannot be applied to the robot. There-
fore, novel variable stiffness methods for flexible robots have
been proposed [22], including implanting low-melting-point ma-
terial (LMPM) or shape-memory material (SMM), using jamming
or lockable mechanisms, etc. In the following sections, these
commonly used variable stiffness methods for flexible robots
have been categorized and elaborately introduced, along with
interesting applications.

blocks.text: 1.3. Scope of article

lines.text: 1.3. Scope of article

blocks.text:
In this paper, we focus on development, challenges, and fu-
ture of the variable stiffness methods for flexible MIS robots.
Common variable stiffness methods are categorized based on
their fundamental principle of altering robot’s stiffness, and the
characteristics of each method are elucidated, which can help
readers understand how to select the suitable methods. After
summarizing the challenges and requirements of current variable
stiffness methods, we introduced two potential methods with
great properties, which may aid users in exploring the ideal
method.

blocks.text: 2.1. Antagonism of internal force

lines.text: 2.1. Antagonism of internal force

blocks.text:
Changing antagonism of the actuators is the most common
way to change stiffness of the structure in nature. For example,
human muscles on the both sides control the joint to rotate
oppositely. When the two groups of muscles contract at the same
time, the overall external stiffness of the joint will increase sig-
nificantly. With the same principle, to adjust the flexible robot’s
stiffness, researchers can enhance the internal force, like increas-
ing the actuation forces simultaneously, to mitigate the influence
caused by external disturbance forces, as shown in Fig. 3(a).

lines.text: Changing antagonism of the actuators is the most common
way to change stiffness of the structure in nature. For example,
human muscles on the both sides control the joint to rotate
oppositely. When the two groups of muscles contract at the same
time, the overall external stiffness of the joint will increase sig-
nificantly. With the same principle, to adjust the flexible robot’s
stiffness, researchers can enhance the internal force, like increas-
ing the actuation forces simultaneously, to mitigate the influence
caused by external disturbance forces, as shown in Fig. 3(a).

blocks.text:
Many proposed flexible surgical robots have used this princi-
ple to vary stiffness. Falco et al. [23] designed a variable stiffness
percutaneous needle for minimally invasive surgery, as shown
in Fig. 4(a). The variation of tendons tension can adjust the
stiffness of robot, which is suitable for puncturing different tissue.
Kim et al. [9] designed a hyper-redundant tubular manipulator
composed of special shape links, which can achieve variable
neutral-line during moving, as shown in Fig. 4(b). With these
links, the robot can achieve continuously changed stiffness by
varying the tension of tendons even during moving. Wakimoto
et al. [29] designed an intestine endoscope like continuum robot
with fiber-reinforced rubber tubes inside, as shown in Fig. 4(d).
As air is pumped in, the pressure of the tube increases to resist
bending, and the robot’s body is stiffened. Huh et al. [24] designed
a compressible tendon driven continuum manipulator, as shown
in Fig. 4(f). With the Increase in internal force and the compres-
sion of consecutive soft joints, the variation in stiffness of robot
body can reach up to approximately fifty times. The antagonism
of hybrid actuation forces is also utilized. Maghooa et al. [28] and
Stilli et al. [27] proposed continuum manipulators with hybrid
actuation which incorporates tendons and pneumatics, as shown
in Fig. 4(c) and (e). Stiffness of the manipulators can be changed
continuously under the antagonism of actuation forces containing
the tension of tendons and the inside air pressure.

In addition to regulating the antagonistic actuation, antago-
nism of robot’s internal forces can also be adjusted by inserting
external components with high elastic modulus. For example,
when a flexible robot exhibits low stiffness, inserting an inner
tube with a high elastic modulus can enhance robot’s stiffness
directly. The pulling force of the driving tendons and the elastic
force of the inner tube antagonize each other when the robot
bends, resulting in a high overall stiffness of the robot. Many
methods of enhancing the stiffness of robot by inserting high
elastic modulus components have been practiced. Lloyd et al. [33]
designed a magnetic-actuated robot with variable stiffness, as
shown in Fig. 4(g). The backbone of the robot is a sliding Nitinol
rod. With the cooperation of different insertion length of the
backbone and the application of magnetic field, stiffness of the

blocks.text:
Utilizing antagonism of internal force can enhance the stiffness
of robot body simply, rapidly and continuously, without the need
for complex structural design. However, this method still has
some drawbacks. Firstly, it necessitates continuous energy input
to sustain the high stiffness state of the robot, thereby increasing
the control complexity of the robot. Additionally, antagonistic
forces generated by different actuators or internal components
exhibit strong coupling, amplifying the challenge of precise con-
trol. Furthermore, it lacks an ability to independently adjust the
stiffness of partial robot sections, which limits its applicability in
certain surgical scenarios.

blocks.text: 2.2. Constraint of relative motion

lines.text: 2.2. Constraint of relative motion

blocks.text:
In many designs of flexible robots, movable structures such as
hinges and sliders are used, and the relative motion between the
movable structures are strongly coupled with the robots’ bending
motions. Researchers have employed diverse methods to impede
the deformation of robot and enhance stiffness by constraining
the relative motion generated inside the movable structures, as
shown in Fig. 3(b). And these motion constraint methods can
be categorized into two groups based on increasing friction and
mechanical engagement, respectively.

achieving the shape locking of robot. Brancadoro et al. [41] pro-

2.2.2. Mechanical engagement (locking)
In addition to jam of small objects, engageable mechanisms
are also used to lock robot’s shape for varying stiffness. Rela-
tive movement occurs between the internal moveable parts of
engageable mechanisms which is coupled with the deforma-
tion of robot body. Then the actuator drives the mechanism to
engage, locking the shape of robot and increasing the overall
stiffness. Comparing with other variable stiffness methods, en-
gageable mechanisms can provide a more reliable shape locking,
which depends on the utilized material.

Liu et al. [55] designed a reversible shape-locking mecha-
nism which can be placed along the flexible robot, as shown in
Fig. 5(e). The mechanism comprises buckles and bellows, which
can engage together and lock the robot’s shape under pneumatic
actuation. Lin et al. [59] designed a modular lockable joint for
flexible surgical robots, as shown in Fig. 5(f). With remote actu-
ation by tendon driving, each joint can be locked and unlocked
independently, and the joint’s state can be maintained with-
out continuous energy input, which provide robot more possible
movements. Pogue et al. [58] proposed a novel magnetic lock-
ing mechanism for tendon-driven continuum robot, as shown in
Fig. 5(g). Under the actuation of external magnetic field, a rotary
plate inside the mechanism would rotate and engage with beads
on the rope that pass through the mechanism, then the robot’s
shape is locked. Wang et al. [81] proposed a tendon-driven robot
with lockable mechanism based on worm gear. Each joint has an
individual SMA trigger to actuate locking motion, and robot can
go inside human body to carry out surgeries with only one motor.

In addition to stable shape locking and a wider range of stiff-
ness change, engageable mechanisms also have other advantages.
Many mechanisms can maintain the engagement individually,
which reduces the coupling between stiffness adjustment and
robot actuation, allowing for a wider range of robot movements
and expanding the workspace. Clark et al. [82] researched the
working modes of a flexible robot with shape-locking mecha-
nism, showed that the proposed robot can not only mimic the
working modes of typical robot arms, such as PUMA, SCARA, and
SPHERICAL, but also work as a general articulated one. Wock-
enfußet al. [83] designed a continuum robot with pneumatic
shape-locking mechanism, and used only two motors to drive it
bending in complex shapes with large workspace.

for small scale flexible robots. Moreover, they may require bulky
external driving modules, such as motors and air pumps, which
increases the complexity and footprint of robot system.

blocks.text:
2.3.1. Phase transition materials
Phase transition materials, such as low-melting-point alloy
(LMPA) and shape-memory-alloy (SMA), can change its stiffness
with joule heat input, which are widely integrated into the robot
to enable stiffness adjustment. There are many low-cost phase
transition materials with different properties, such as wax and
shape memory nickel titanium alloy, on the market, which pro-
vide researchers diverse choice. Since these materials can provide
considerable stiffness variation, they can be applied to flexi-
ble surgical robots with small outer diameters, such as catheter
robots.

blocks.text:
Kim et al. [75] designed a novel flexible robot for MRI-guided
neurosurgery, as shown in Fig. 6(a). The robot’s body is composed
of consecutive SMA springs. The SMA spring exists in austenite
phase in high temperature, leading to a low stiffness of robot
body. When heat dissipates and temperature of SMA springs
drops, they transform to martensite phase and become harder, re-
sulting in a high stiffness of robot body. Wang et al. [61] proposed
a controllable stiffness manipulation arm with phase-change ma-
terial filling inside the gap of joints, as shown in Fig. 6(b). With a
large area rolling electric heating film and water cooling system,
the phase-change material can switching between liquid and
solid phases to meet different stiffness needs. Piskarev et al. [72]
proposed a magnetic catheter with a variable stiffness outer tube
made of shape memory polymer PTFE(polytetrafluoroethylene),
as shown in Fig. 6(c). The fabrication process of PTFE tube con-
tains repeat dipping and curing, which allows the tube to be thin
for the neurosurgery. Internal helical copper electrode can heat
the tube, causing it to soften and allowing the robot to be flexible.
Meanwhile, the hollow backbone can serve as a cooling channel
to dissipate heat from the tube, thereby stiffening the robot. Le
et al. [12] designed a continuum robot with four PET tubes inside,
as shown in Fig. 6(d). Each tube has a flexible stainless steel
sheath embedded in it to work as a heating element, which help
the tube transform from stiff glass state to soft rubbery state to
vary robot’s stiffness. And cooling air goes through the channel of
PET tube to actively and safely remove the heat for making robot
stiff again. Farshid et al. [66] designed a two-segment continuum
robot with spring embedded as elastic backbone, as shown in
Fig. 6(e). The spring has been coated with PTFE, and multiple
sets of electrical wires are placed inside to control the location
of being soft.

blocks.text:
However, some factors of using these materials should be
considered. Heat is needed for these materials when changing
their stiffness, and the temperature of material may be higher
than 41 ◦C, which is the threshold of scald of human body. What
is more, the heating and heat dissipation process takes from 10 s
to several hundred seconds, which is not suitable for adjusting the
stiffness of robot frequently during surgery. Therefore, in addition
to the compact heating system, a heat dissipation system is also
required, which is critical to improving the working efficiency
of the robot, while it also increases the complexity of the robot
design and poses a challenge to the miniaturization of the robot
system.

Gaeta et al. [76] designed a soft robot with variable stiffness
by combining magneto-rheological fluid and particle jamming, as
shown in Fig. 6(g). With the application of an external magnetic
field, particles in the magneto-rheological fluid align in chains
and cling to the layers inside the robot. The shear force of the fluid
increases, resulting in an enhancement of friction between layers,
leading to an improved jamming effect and effectively altering
the stiffness of the robot.

blocks.text:

are summarized, and two potential variable stiffness method are
introduced. Moreover, the advantages of variable stiffness flexible
robots in avoiding obstacles and following predetermined paths
are discussed.

blocks.text: 3.1. Challenges of current variable stiffness methods

lines.text: 3.1. Challenges of current variable stiffness methods

blocks.text:
Although methods summarized previously can enable the
stiffness variation of flexible MIS robots, they still exhibit several
inevitable drawbacks. Due to the coupling between actuation
forces, utilizing antagonism of internal force to vary stiffness
increases the complexity of precise control for robotic operations,
which would escalate as the number of controllable section
increases. Altering the stiffness of a robot by constraining motions
of internal movable structures, the complexity of these structures
limits their capability of miniaturization. And the engageable
mechanisms only have two states, locked and unlocked, resulting
in their inability to provide continuous change stiffness.

blocks.text:
Using variable stiffness materials also encounters problems.
Robots vary stiffness basing on thermally phase transition materi-
als cannot alter their stiffness frequently, since the materials need
time to be soften and stiffen. And the phase transition points of
many materials are higher than the scald threshold of the human
body, which increases the risk of surgery. For rheological fluids,
altering stiffness requires a good balance between the intensity
of external field and the volume of fluids, and how to remotely
activate the rheological effect of these fluids to vary the stiffness
of a millimeter-level flexible robot deep inside the human body
remains a challenge.

From the perspective of safety, the size of robot is a crucial pa-
rameter that should be considered, then a summary of constraint
of common natural tracts is given out in Table 2, which can be a
reference for designers to determine the maximum size of their
flexible robots. Furthermore, two potential methods that can be
used to vary the stiffness of flexible MIS robots are introduced in
the following section, which are employing electrostatic adhesion
(EA) and non-Newton fluid (NNF), respectively. Variable stiffness
mechanisms based on these two methods have capability to reach
those ideal characteristics mentioned above.

lines.text: 3.2. Potential variable stiffness methods

blocks.text:
3.2.1. Electrostatic adhesion
EA is a widely used method in robotics for adhesion applica-
tion [97]. The EA force, generated from the Johnsen–Rahbek (J–R)
effect, exist between a conductor and a semiconductor when they
are in contact and a voltage is applied across them, as shown in
Fig. 7(a).

by adhering the movable parts and increase the friction [100]. In
addition, EA only actuated by applying voltage on the electrodes
rather than tendon driving or air pumping, which can decouple
the stiffness variation process with actuation of robot bending, as
shown in the example in Fig. 7(b). And the actuation module of
EA based mechanism only contains a electric power and relative
circuit board. Comparing with the common actuation module
that contains a large amount of motors or bulky fluid pump, the
actuation module of EA only contains electric power and circuit
boards, which is small and portable for more possible surgical
scenarios like outdoor emergency surgery.

blocks.text:
However, some challenges may occurred when applying EA on
the flexible surgical robots. The magnitude of EA force is relative
to not only the type and thickness of the material of electrode, but
also the voltage and contacting area [101]. Therefore, in order to
achieve excellent stiffness variation capability in millimeter-level
surgical robots, electrodes with higher dielectric constant should
be invented, and the effective contacting area of electrodes within
the robot body should be enlarged.

3.2.2. Non-Newtonian fluid
Non-Newtonian fluid also has great potential to be used in
the small-scale variable stiffness surgical robots, whose viscosity
depends on the stress on it and does not follow the Newton’s law
of viscosity [102], as shown in Fig. 7(c).

blocks.text:
Some kinds of NNFs shows the characteristic that their vis-
cosity has a positive relationship with the shear rate of itself.
With quickly oscillating external stimuli, these NNFs can rapidly
transition from fluid to solid states, as the jamming of inner tiny
particles, which can be used to vary stiffness of flexible robots.
Xu et al. [99] proposed a novel design of magnetic miniature soft
robot with variable stiffness that base on the NNF, as shown in
Fig. 7(d). A rapidly oscillating external magnetic field is applied to
the robot, and the stiffness of NNF-based robot body is changed,
as the inner particles are resisting the intense interactions.

blocks.text: 3.3. Advantages of variable stiffness flexible robots in motion

lines.text: 3.3. Advantages of variable stiffness flexible robots in motion

blocks.text:
With certain stiffness varying methods, flexible robots can
independently lock parts of the body and keep moving the free
parts, which can achieve novel motions that differentiate them
from previous flexible robots. The control strategy for flexible
robots moving in these type motions has not been extensively
investigated, which presents the potential for these robots to
achieve more precise path-following and enhanced obstacle-
avoidance capabilities [83,103]. The follow-the-leader (FTL) is the
best moving strategy for flexible robot to follow a predetermined
path and avoid obstacles [104]. However, FTL necessitates the
robot to independently and simultaneously control each movable
part, which is hard to be attained for hyper-redundant flexible
surgical robots.

blocks.text: 4. Conclusion

lines.text: 4. Conclusion

blocks.text:
In this review, variable stiffness methods from relative lit-
erature have been categorized into three types based on their
fundamental principles: antagonism of internal force, constraint
of relative motion, and using variable stiffness materials. Each
method is elucidated along with applications, its advantages and
drawbacks are summarized. The characteristics of ideal variable
stiffness method are proposed, and two potential methods are
introduced. Furthermore, the advantages of variable stiffness flex-
ible robot in motion are discussed, which may lead to expanded
exploration of applications of variable stiffness flexible robots
in rescue, manufacturing, outdoor surgery, aerospace, and other
fields.

blocks.text:
Abstract—A ﬂexible surgical robot that can adjust its stiffness
guarantees safe operation by satisfying both the high ﬂexibility
required when the robot approaches a surgical target and the
more stiffness necessary for the end effector to perform surgical
procedures. Therefore, this paper proposes a ﬂexible surgical robot
that consists of a central backbone, eight super-elastic wires as
peripheral backbones, SMA springs, rubber tubes, and several
disks. The inner diameter of the SMA springs that can be changed
via their temperature creates a tightening force change to apply
onto the eight backbone wires of the robot to adjust the overall
stiffness of the robot. The simple structure is favorable for robot
miniaturization. Frictional force and stiffness modulation experi-
ments of the robot are performed. The results conﬁrmed that the
robot’s stiffness was increased approximately 1.4 times between
the martensite state and the austenite state of the SMA spring. The
relationship model between the ﬂexural rigidity of the robot and
the frictional force between the SMA spring with the peripheral
backbones is established. We compared the ﬂexural rigidity values
obtained from our model with those of the experimental result and
conﬁrmed that the model was valid.

can perform various surgical procedures, including access to
a lesion, incision, and suturing, within a limited operating space
because it can be bent inside the human body, unlike long and
rigid surgical tools. SPL using a ﬂexible surgical robot has the
advantage of providing patients with a small scar, little pain, and
short-term recovery, although SPL still has some drawbacks,
such as the cost of the instruments, the length of the operation,
and the surgeon’s operational complexity. Considering the re-
quired diameter, length, and end effector force for each surgical
ﬁeld, ﬂexible surgical robots have been researched in vari-
ous surgical ﬁelds, including otolaryngology surgery [1], brain
surgery [2], [3], cardiovascular surgery [4]–[6], gastrointestinal
surgery [7], [8], and natural oriﬁce transluminal endoscopic
surgery [9]–[12]. To perform robotic surgery with a ﬂexible
robot in a limited ﬁeld of view, it is necessary to sense the
robot shape and track the position of the robot’s tip. However,
the greater DOF in a ﬂexible robot, the more difﬁcult it is to
sense the robot shape and precise control. Therefore, to improve
the control stability of a ﬂexible robot, medical imaging sys-
tems such as computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), and ultrasound (US) have been used for robotic
surgery. In particular, MRI has a high resolution and ensures
patient safety, while US has a low resolution, and CT has a
problem of allergic reactions and organ damage in patients
becauseofcontrastagentsandradiation.InanMRIenvironment,
the materials of a ﬂexible surgical robot must be compatible with
an electromagnetic ﬁeld. However, most metals cause noise in
MRI and are not suitable for ﬂexible surgical robot materials.
Some materials with MRI compatibility, such as brass [13],
shape memory alloys (SMAs) [14]–[17], silicone rubber [18],
and plastics [15], have been used for ﬂexible surgical robots
with MRI guidance. Among them, SMA is a biocompatible
material used in many surgical robots in MRI environments. An
SMA also has a high-power density. Thus, it is used to create
compact actuators for miniaturization and weight reduction
in surgical robots or grippers. Kim et al. developed an SMA
spring-based active stiffness continuum robot for neurosurgery
and conﬁrmed its MRI compatibility [14]. The high ﬂexibility
of the robot allows it to move smoothly without any injury to
a lesion. However, its stability might be reduced because low
stiffness could bring about undesirable deformation or bending.
In addition, the insufﬁcient stiffness of the robot limits the end
effectorforce,whichisrequiredwhentherobotperformsvarious
operations, such as incision and suturing. As a result, it is nec-
essary to control the stiffness of the robot based on the speciﬁc
scenario.

JEON et al.: TOWARDS A SNAKE-LIKE FLEXIBLE ROBOT WITH VARIABLE STIFFNESS

lines.text: JEON et al.: TOWARDS A SNAKE-LIKE FLEXIBLE ROBOT WITH VARIABLE STIFFNESS

blocks.text:
Many studies have been conducted to realize stiffness con-
trol. Cianchetti et al. proposed a manipulator for minimal ac-
cess surgery that can implement selective stiffness changes by
combining a ﬂuid actuator to enable omnidirectional bending,
elongation functionality, and jamming [18], [19]. Jiang et al.
proposed a high DOF variable stiffness mechanism that can be
highly refracted. The rigidity of each joint can be independently
controlled using the jamming principle through vacuum gener-
ation, and the effect of vacuum pressure and particle type on
stiffness adjustment can be studied [20]. Kim et al. proposed a
stiffness conversion mechanism layer jamming through friction
between the layers of a snake-shaped hollow manipulator com-
posed of several layers of thin mylar ﬁlm and tested the stiffness
andfracturestrengthofthelayerjamming[21],[22].Moses etal.
[23] proposed a stiffness control manipulator whose main body
includes thirty interlocking ﬁbers and a ﬂexible sheath around
the manipulator. The ﬁbers are free to slide along the ﬂexible
sheath that may be evacuated to increase its stiffness. Although
granular and layer jamming approaches achieve signiﬁcant stiff-
ness, the system still requires a large volume or layered structure
to achieve adequate stiffness. Kim et al. proposed a mechanism
to adjust the joint stiffness of a robot with a thin tubular structure
through a unique asymmetric arrangement between the tendons
and the links and combined this with a change in wire tension
[24]. This structure approaches have the advantage of being able
to switch between ﬂexible and stiff modes quickly. However,
the tendons’ tension must be high, and the links must be strong
enough to ensure enough friction to keep the rigidity. Kim et al.
proposed a mechanism to control the stiffness by overlapping
the segment of the inner tube and the segment of the outer tube
through relative translational and rotational movements between
patterned coaxial tubes [25]. Even though its stiffness can be
changed quickly, the robot may be twisted when the tubes are
rotated to change their stiffness. Le et al. proposed a manipulator
consisting of PET and stainless-steel sheaths that controlled the
rigidity through heating, and the rigidity increased by at least
nine times [26]. When heated to 70 °C or higher, the PET will
produce toxic pyrolysis products. Jiang et al. [27] presented a
variable stiffness for continuum manipulator using an SMA-
based sheath. However, the restoring force of the SMA-based
sheath will be disturbed the bending motion of the robot, and
the mesh surface of the sheath will not be arranged regularly and
uniformly on the mesh surface when this structure is bent.

As a result, this paper proposes a stiffness control mecha-
nism for a multi-backbone snake-like robot based on an SMA
spring to address these limitations. The proposed robot has
three characteristics. First, the robot has a relatively simple
structure compared to previous studies, which includes an SMA
spring inserted into a robot composed of several disks, a cen-
tral backbone, a rubber tube, and eight super-elastic wires as
peripheral backbones. Second, the SMA spring is used as an
actuator that applies a strong tightening force to the peripheral
backbones when a current is applied. Third, the core principle
of this stiffness control system is the frictional force between
the rubber layer and the peripheral backbones generated by
the tightening force of the SMA spring. The stiffness control
mechanism produces sufﬁcient stiffness and stiffness range
within a simple structure. The stiffness of the robot will be
modeled using the energy equation containing frictional work,
stored spring energy, and work of an external force applied to
the robot. In Section II, we discuss the design of the proposed
robot. We present the stiffness modeling to verify the effect of

blocks.text: II. DESIGN AND WORKING PRINCIPLE OF A SURGICAL ROBOT

lines.text: II. DESIGN AND WORKING PRINCIPLE OF A SURGICAL ROBOT

blocks.text: A. Design and Working Principle

lines.text: A. Design and Working Principle

blocks.text:
Our surgical robot was designed based on the multi-backbone
snake-like robot [28] proposed by Simaan et al. The surgical
robot consists of three segments, including four disks, a central
backbone, four tendons, and several wires as peripheral back-
bones, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The central backbone is attached
to the center of all disks to keep a constant distance between the
disks and prevent rotation of disks. The wires at the peripheral
backbones are only linked to the base disk so that they can
slide freely through the other disks when the robot is bent.
In Fig. 1(b), each disk has four tendon holes, one hole for the
central backbone and several holes for the peripheral backbone
wires. A rubber tube covers the center segment of the peripheral
backbones and the SMA spring is wound on the outside of the
rubber tube. A current is applied to the SMA spring through
conductive threads attached to both ends to raise its temperature,
as shown in Fig. 1(c).

An SMA has different lattice structures and phases depending
on its temperature. It includes a martensite phase with a face-
centered cubic crystal structure at a low temperature and an
austenite phase with a body-centered cubic crystal structure at a
high temperature. When the SMA is deformed in the martensite
phase, the structure of the crystal lattice is deformed, but the
bonds between atoms are not broken. The structure of the crystal
lattice is transformed from twinned martensite to detwinned
martensite. After that, as the temperature of the SMA increases,
the detwinned martensite changes to austenite lattice structure.
As a result, the SMA is restored to its original shape. As the

a relatively large diameter (Df), as shown in Fig. 1(d). When the
phase of the SMA changes to the full austenite phase through
heating, it generates a tightening force on the rubber tube in the
radial direction to restore the original smaller diameter (D0 <
Df = Drb), as shown in Fig. 1(e). This force (FT) will tighten
the rubber tube to increase the frictional force (Ff) between the
rubber tube and peripheral backbones. This tightening force
can be changed depending on the phase of the SMA spring.
When the phase of the SMA spring changes into martensite
through natural cooling, the force starts to decrease, and the
SMA spring has a relatively weak tightening force on the rubber
tube to reduce the frictional force. The core of the proposed
stiffness control mechanism is the frictional force generated
through the tightening force between the SMA spring and the
rubber tube. The frictional force increases the robot stiffness
by restraining the movement of the peripheral backbones that
could relatively freely slide with the rubber and disks as the
robot bends, as shown in Fig. 1(f). The diameter of the rubber
tube (the outer diameter of the peripheral backbones) is also an
important variable affecting the tightening force. As mentioned,
the tightening force can be adjusted based on the phase change
of the SMA spring. Therefore, the stiffness of the robot can be
controlled based on the phase of the SMA spring.

blocks.text:
Two pairs of opposing tendons embedded in the disks of the
ﬂexible surgical robot can control its bending in two directions.
The tendons are ﬁxed to only the end disk, and they can move
freely on the other disks. When one of the tendon pairs is
pulled, the space between the disks along that tendon decreases,
while the distance between the disks along the opposing tendon
increases. As a result, the ﬂexible surgical robot is bent in this
direction, as shown in Fig. 1(f). Similarly, the ﬂexible surgical
robot is bent in the second direction perpendicular to the ﬁrst
via another pair of tendons.

material with a thickness of 2 mm is used for the robot’s disks.

used as the peripheral backbones of the robot. A rubber tube with
a thickness of 0.25 mm is inserted between the SMA spring and
the peripheral backbones to increase the frictional force. Acrylic
material with a thickness of 2 mm is used for the robot’s disks.

In Fig. 2(a), two robots with four and eight peripheral back-
bones were used for the stiffness experiment with a load of
500 g at both martensite and austenite states to determine the
proper number of backbones. As a result, we selected the robot
with eight backbones that showed more stiffness conversion
capability than the robot with four backbones. In addition, the
number of coils of the SMA spring is an important variable that
affects the stiffness control capability of the robot. However,
an SMA spring with many turns complicates the modeling by
causing undesired deformation in the peripheral backbones.
Therefore, in this paper, experiments and analysis were per-
formed using an SMA spring with 1.5 turns to exclude modeling
errors caused by the deformation of the peripheral backbones.
Finally, we performed a preliminary test of the bending capacity
of the robot. In Fig. 2(b), driving the robot using the polyethylene
thread as a tendon proved that the robot can be bent up to 90° in
the vertical, left, and right directions.

We analyzed how the robot’s stiffness changed due to the
frictional force between the rubber tube and the peripheral
backbones using the work-energy equation. It was used by Allen
Jiang et al. for simulation in the jamming mechanism, one of
the variable stiffness mechanisms [20]. The work done by the
external force in a cantilever beam would be the sum of the
stiffness element’s stored spring energy (U) and friction energy
loss caused by the frictional force between the internal particles.

blocks.text:
The stiffness of the robot should be changed depending on
the application scenario, and the range and maximum value of
the stiffness of the robot are important parameters that need
to be studied. In this paper, the stiffness is controlled by the
friction force between the rubber tube and the eight peripheral
backbones based on (9). This friction force can be adjusted
using the clamping force of the SMA spring, which covers the
outside of the rubber tube. The range and maximum values of
the friction force are determined by the outer backbone diameter
(Dt) and the inner diameter of the SMA spring (D0), as shown
in Fig. 1(b) and (e). Therefore, in this section, the friction force
and the stiffness are determined and evaluated with robots in
three different conﬁgurations with outer peripheral backbone
diameters of 5.5 mm, 5.75 mm, and 6 mm. The ﬂexural rigidity

experiments. Then, this calculated ﬂexural rigidity is compared

force between one wire and the rubber layer will be investigated

phase. In the experimental setup shown in Fig. 4(a), the rubber
tube wraps around the eight wires of the robot. A single wire
is attached to the moving disk and can move through the ﬁxing
disk and the rest of the (seven) wires are ﬁxed to the ﬁxing
disk and not attached to the moving disk. When the micro-linear
actuator moves, the force sensor will pull the moving disk with
the PE thread. The single wire will move with the moving disk
and slide on the rubber layer that is held by the other seven
wires, as shown in Fig. 4(b). Thus, we measured the friction
force via the force sensor. The micro-linear actuator moves the

disk are shown in Fig. 4(c)–(e) for the three conﬁgurations (the
three peripheral backbone outer diameters). The results show
that the friction force of the SMA spring in the austenite state
is higher than that in the martensite state. The ratio between the
maximum friction forces in the austenite and martensite state
was 1.54, 1.48, and 1.39 times for diameters of 5.5, 5.75, and
6 mm, respectively. The maximum and mean values of friction
forces are summarized with the backbone diameter in Table I.
As the backbone diameter increases, the friction increases. This
tendency is because of the larger backbone diameter, which
results in a greater tightening force when an identical SMA
spring was used. As a result, it can be predicted that the robot

blocks.text: C. SMA Spring Thermo-Mechanical Behaviors

lines.text: C. SMA Spring Thermo-Mechanical Behaviors

blocks.text:
The thermal behaviors of the SMA spring are investigated in
terms of heating and cooling time. As shown in Fig. 6(a), an
infrared (thermal) camera monitors temperature changes during
heating and cooling processes at the SMA spring, while a video
camera records the temperature indicator on the thermal camera.
TheheatingprocessoftheSMAspringisrepeatedthreetimesfor
the three different electric current values. The average heating
rates are shown in Fig. 6(b). Using 0.5 A, 0.4 A and 0.3 A, the
SMA spring was heated from 25 °C to 60 °C in about 18, 21 and
115 seconds, respectively. The ambient cooling process of the
SMA spring is also performed three times as shown in Fig. 6(c).
The results show that the cooling time took approximately 60 s.
It is noted that the thermal behaviors of the SMA springs with
three backbone diameters are almost identical. Fig. 6(d) shows
time-lapse thermal images of the heating and cooling processes
occurring on the SMA spring. Although the SMA spring was
maintained around 70 °C for 5 minutes, the temperature on the
robot’s surface does not exceed 37.5 °C as Fig. 6(e). The thermal
image of the robot at 71.4 °C and 37.4 °C were compared to
demonstrate that the high temperature of the SMA spring does
not affect the human body.

blocks.text: V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION

lines.text: V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION

blocks.text:
In this study, we developed a ﬂexible surgical robot whose
stiffness can be controlled to prevent a lack of stability due
to insufﬁcient stiffness of the robot when used in single-port
laparoscopy. The simple structure of the robot includes a central
backbone, several acrylic disks, eight super-elastic wires, SMA
springs, andarubber tube. TheSMAspringthat wraps therubber
tube generates a tightening force on the rubber to increase the
frictional force. This frictional force restrains the movement of
the super-elastic wires to increase the stiffness of the robot. The
tightening force of the SMA spring can be changed with the
change phase effect caused by a temperature change (martensite
and austenite states).

to insufﬁcient stiffness of the robot when used in single-port
laparoscopy. The simple structure of the robot includes a central
backbone, several acrylic disks, eight super-elastic wires, SMA
springs, andarubber tube. TheSMAspringthat wraps therubber
tube generates a tightening force on the rubber to increase the
frictional force. This frictional force restrains the movement of
