Assumption 3 is based from the fact that the elongation-rates were slow and the temperature
transients were small for this set of experiments. The temperature of even the complete 1×27
cable only deviated from ambient air temperature by less than ±1 °C. We additionally expect
radial temperature gradients in individual wires and between adjacent layers can be neglected.
Treating the cable as a monolithic element, the Biot number is low Bi = hD/kM = 0.017 ≪1,
where h = 90 Wm−2K−1) is a conservatively high convective ﬁlm coeﬃcient for stagnant air,
D = 1.582 mm is the specimen diameter, and kM = 8.6 Wm−1K−1 is the conductivity of martensite
(lower than austenite). This calculation ignores the fact that conduction is limited to the contact
patches between the wires, but even a ten-fold decrease in eﬀective kM still results in Bi ≪1.

We ﬁrst consider the innermost two components of the 1×27 cable. The deduced global me-

piecing together relevant segments of responses of Figs. 6 (core wire, cycles 1 through 3) and 7
(1×6 strand, cycles 1 and 2). These estimate the isothermal responses that would be measured if
the specimens were simply elongated to δe/Le = 10 % and back to zero load without interruption.

Figure 11 reveals why certain features in the axial force and torque responses of the 1×6 strand
do not line up, such as the lengths and termination points of the axial load and torque plateaus.
In particular, the 1×6 axial load (Fig. 11a) suddenly increases at δe/Le = 6.0 % (termination of
the loading plateau), but the torque (Fig. 11b) remains smooth and does not stiﬀen until beyond
δe/Le = 8 %. Here, we see the core wire is solely responsible for the kink in the 1×6 strand
force response, since the subtraction removed any such kink from the force response layer B. The
apparent force plateau in layer B continues smoothly until about δe/Le = 8 % before the response
takes a gentle upturn, all of which are now mirrored in the torque response at the same elongation
values. Presumably, the “easy” portion of R+ →M+ transformation in the helical wires of layer
B starts at δe/Le = 2.2 % and does not complete until about 8 to 9 % strain. Similar characteristic
strain values can be identiﬁed for the M+ →R+ transformation during unloading, since the force
and torque plateaus (and other features) in layer B are now well correlated. Thus, we expect the

4.2.2. Layer C
The deduced response of layer C is obtained by subtracting the 1×6 response (Exp. S2a) from
the 1×15 response (Exp. M2a), and is shown in Fig. 12. As before for clarity, only the outer
envelope of cycle 1 and 2 are shown for the un-normalized force and torque responses (Figs. 12a
and 12b). Figures 12c and 12d, however, show the normalized force and torque responses of layer
C response during cycles 1 and cycle 2 and the loading portion of cycle 3. These were normalized
by the reference area and torsion constant of layer C alone. The 1×6 strand failed during cycle 3,
so no subtraction was possible for unloading. The circled labels in Figs. 12c and 12d correspond
to the strain ﬁeld images of the 1×15 (Exp. M2a) in Fig. 9c during cycle 3 loading.

blocks.text: Several confusing aspects of the previous 1×15 results are resolved by the response subtraction.

lines.text: Several confusing aspects of the previous 1×15 results are resolved by the response subtraction.

blocks.text:
1. During initial loading (below δe/Le = 6 %), the 1×15 torque (Fig. 12b) was slightly wavy
with a knee in the torque at about δe/Le = 1 %, yet the DIC strain ﬁelds were relatively
uniform (between 1 and 2 in Fig. 9c). After subtraction, the inferred torque of layer C
is much smoother, with a monotonically decreasing tangent modulus up to the local torque
maximum at δe/Le = 6.0 %.
2. The 1×15 torque had a local maximum at δe/Le = 6.0 % where strain localizations began to
appear between 2 and 3 , yet the axial load tangent modulus was relatively constant across
this point. After subtraction, layer C’s axial force and torque tangent moduli both change
together at δe/Le = 6.0 % in Figs. 12a and 12b. What made this particularly confusing before
was that the termination of the force plateau in the core wire occurred at δe/Le = 6.0 %,
coincidentally the same point as the onset of R+ →M+ transformation in layer C (see again
Fig. 9c).
3. The 1×15 axial load exhibited a relatively constant slope between δe/Le = 8 and 20 %, yet
the torque had a local minimum near δe/Le = 15 %. After subtraction, layer C’s axial load
and torque both stiﬀen together. As one expects, the mechanical stiﬀening now coincides
with the disappearance of low strain regions in Fig. 9c ( 5 through 7 ). Furthermore, the
1×15 torque (Fig. 12b) had a relatively constant negative slope between δe/Le = 6 and 11 %,
but thereafter drops more steeply (at least initially) due to the stiﬀening in the 1×6 negative
torque’s contribution. After subtraction, this kink in the torque response at 11 % is removed
in layer C’s torque response.

Incidentally, a small spike appears during cycle 1 in the normalized axial load (Fig. 12c) just
after the maximum value of δe/Le. This spike is an artifact of subtracting two response curves that
did not have the exact same maximum strain. The 1×15 specimen was stretched to δe/Le = 6.98 %,
but the 1×6 specimen was stretched slightly further to δe/Le = 7.12 %, so the subtraction is
inaccurate between these strains.

4.2.3. Layer D
The deduced response of the outermost layer D, shown in Fig. 13, was obtained by subtracting
the response of the 1×15 strand from the response of the full 1×27 cable. Again, the thin lines
in Figs. 13a and 13b are the measured outer envelopes (cycles 1 to 3) of the raw force and torque
responses, respectively, while the bold lines are the subtracted response of layer D. Normalized
force and torque responses for layer D, showing loading and unloading cycles 1 through 3, are
provided in Figs. 13c and 13d. Note that during cycle 3 unloading, the subtracted response of layer
D is incomplete because the 1×15 strand reached zero load at δe/Le = 10.5 %, at which point the
1×27 cable still carried 48 N of load.

4.3. Comparison of 1×27 components and layers
Finally, a comparison of the normalized mechanical responses of the four 1×27 components
and the three helical layers are summarized in Fig. 14. Measured force and torque response (nor-
malized) are shown in Figs. 14a and 14b, respectively. Deduced (subtracted) force and torque
normalized responses of helical wire layers A, B, and C are shown respectively in Figs. 14c and
14d. Except for the core wire response, which shows only cycle 1, all other components and layer
responses are outer envelopes of cycles 1 and 2. Figure 14a shows the clear progression to more
compliant behavior in the normalized force responses from the core wire, 1×6 strand, 1×15 strand,
to the full 1×27 cable. Although the torque responses alternate sign, the magnitude of the normal-
ized torque responses follow the same progression. On a normalized basis, the 1×6 strand exhibits
the greatest torque magnitude, and the full cable exhibits the least.

Before concluding, we should comment on the utility of subtracting the mechanical responses
of components to infer the response of wire layers. Clearly, it is not a substitute for direct mea-
surement. Even if our assumptions are perfectly satisﬁed, subtracting experimental data always
magniﬁes errors. On the other hand, we found it useful to illuminate important features in the
behavior without a large experimental eﬀort. For example, in our early full 1×27 experiments (see
Fig. 6a and Fig. 14 in Part I) we performed IR imaging without DIC. During loading, the axial
stress tangent modulus changed at δe/Le = 1.2 %, but remained relatively constant beyond that.
Similarly, the IR images showed a spatially uniform temperature ﬁeld, which remained temporally
constant beyond δe/Le = 1.2 % (see Fig. 14c in Part I). Between δe/Le = 1.2 % and 12 %, it
was quite diﬃcult to determine when individual layers transformed. After performing experiments
on the hierarchy of components of the 1×27 cable and subtracting the mechanical responses, the
initial knee in the full cable’s response at δe/Le = 1.2 % was determined to be due to A →R+

blocks.text: 5. Summary & Conclusions

lines.text: 5. Summary & Conclusions

blocks.text:
In Part I of this two part series, two shape memory alloy cable designs, a 7×7×0.275 mm and
1×27×0.226 mm construction, were introduced. Here in Part II, the cables were disassembled to
examine the superelastic behavior of their sub-components at nearly isothermal loading rates. The
signiﬁcant conclusions are as follows:

lines.text: In Part I of this two part series, two shape memory alloy cable designs, a 7×7×0.275 mm and
1×27×0.226 mm construction, were introduced. Here in Part II, the cables were disassembled to
examine the superelastic behavior of their sub-components at nearly isothermal loading rates. The
signiﬁcant conclusions are as follows:

blocks.text:
1. The 1×7 core stand and full 7×7 cable had similar isothermal mechanical responses to that
of the straight core wire. This similarity is largely due to the small helix angles in the
design, which causes the wires to be loaded predominately in tension. As such, all three
components exhibited propagating transformation fronts. Certain detailed observations were
new, however, such as the staggered wire fronts in the 1×7 strand.
2. SMA cables are highly tailorable by their design, as illustrated by the wide range of mechan-
ical responses from each of the 1×27 components. For example, the tensile secant modulus
at δe/Le = 2 % strain was 23.7, 18.4, 11.1, and 7.3 GPa for the core wire, 1×6, 1×15, and
1×27 cable, respectively, while the strain at failure (at the grips) was 11.2 %, 16.4 %, 29.3 %,
and 39.2 %, respectively. Similar to a spring, one can trade force for displacement.
3. Aside from the core wire, no propagating transformation fronts were detected in the 1×27
cable or its multi-layered subcomponents. Although some localized strain and temperature
characteristics were measured by stereo digital image correlation (DIC) and infrared imag-
ing, these features never propagated during phase transformation. The origin of this behavior
was traced to pre-existing indents (contact stress concentrations) between adjacent wire lay-
ers, arising from the cable’s manufacturing process. Localizations were evenly distributed
along the specimen length (due to the pattern of many indents), and they slowly grew and

Since this is the ﬁrst detailed experimental study of SMA cables to our knowledge, we con-
clude this article series with some comments on potential future work. Overall, the prospects for
new applications of SMA cables appears bright, yet challenging. The two cable designs stud-
ied herein provide an idea of the breadth of mechanical responses oﬀered by SMA cables, but a
myriad of other possible cable cross-sections, alloy compositions, and lays remain to be explored.
Faced with a multitude of options, the design engineer will need reliable modeling/computational
tools to predict the behavior of new designs. This is a challenging prospect since three dimen-
sional polycrystalline SMA constitutive models are still maturing (Lagoudas et al., 2006), and
tension/torsion/bending data on (even initially straight) SMA wires are rare. Furthermore, while
we focused on the superelastic behavior of these SMA cables due to their sub-ambient (stress-free)
transformation temperatures, SMA cables do indeed exhibit the shape memory eﬀect if suﬃciently
cooled (Reedlunn et al., 2009). SMA cables made of diﬀerent NiTi alloys with elevated transfor-
mation temperatures could certainly be used as thermally-responsive, high-tension actuators. As
previously mentioned in Part I, the cable form of SMAs should enable the future development of
cost-eﬀective, ﬂexible (in bending/twisting), and highly tailorable actuators. SMA cable actuators
in prosthetic limbs (Bundhoo et al., 2009), for example, could be bent around tight hinge radii and
designed to give the precise force-displacement response necessary to give the prosthetic a natu-
ral feel. Future research in experiments and modeling, while demanding, would be a worthwhile
endeavor, as we have as yet only scratched the surface of the potential utility of SMA cables.

lines.text: A Biologically Inspired Wet Shape Memory Alloy

lines.text: Actuated Robotic Pump

blocks.text: Matthew D. Pierce and Stephen A. Mascaro, Member, IEEE

lines.text: Matthew D. Pierce and Stephen A. Mascaro, Member, IEEE

blocks.text:
Abstract—This paper presents the concept, design, optimiza-
tion, and experimental analysis of a biologically inspired wet shape
memory alloy (SMA) actuated pump for robotic and mechatronic
systems. Just as the human heart provides energy to the muscles in
the body, the robotic SMA pump distributes thermoﬂuidic energy
to arrays of SMA actuators that function as robotic muscles. Fur-
thermore, the robotic pump draws from its own ﬂuidic output to
assist in the actuation of its own internal SMA actuators, just as a
portion of the blood pumped by the human heart supplies energy
to its own muscles. A feasibility analysis provides insight to lim-
its of conﬁguration parameters. Through dynamic modeling and
simulation of the system, various conﬁgurations can be analyzed
for optimization of the output. The effects of changing conﬁgura-
tion parameters were explored via simulation and validated with
experimentation. The current prototype of the SMA heart is capa-
ble of pumping 2.1 times more ﬂuid than is required to sustain its
own actuation. This is the ﬁrst successful implementation of such a
robotic pump, such that it has a net positive thermoﬂuidic output
to provide to other actuators while sustaining its own actuation via
thermoﬂuidic feedback. Furthermore, this SMA pump is capable
of pumping a net output of 66 mL/min, which is two orders of
magnitude larger than the output of any other SMA pump.

blocks.text:
S ROBOTIC and mechatronic systems become increas-
ingly inspired by biological systems, the need for bioin-
spired actuation technologies increases. Common methods of
actuation include the use of electrical motors, pneumatics, and
hydraulics. The use of smart materials such as electroactive
polymers and shape memory alloys (SMAs) are becoming in-
creasingly popular in robotics due to their resemblance to muscle
[1] and their biocompatibility [2]. These properties make them
good candidates for hand and facial prosthetics research [3], [4].
In addition to their biocompatibility, there are also many other
advantages to using SMA actuators for nonbiological mecha-
nisms including thermostats [5], adaptive wings [6], and even
humanoid robots [7], [8].

blocks.text:
SMAs are commonly used for applications that do not require
high reciprocation rates due to their limited bandwidth. This is
due to the difﬁculty of heating and cooling the SMA quickly and
efﬁciently. For this reason, the wet SMA actuator was developed
to allow for more efﬁcient actuation and increased rates using
forced convection by using both thermoﬂuidic and electrical
heating [9]. Fig. 1 shows a diagram of the wet SMA actuator
concept. A wet SMA actuator consists of SMA wire enveloped in
ﬂuid that is contained within a compliant tube. This compliance
allows for the actuator to expand and contract with minimal
spring resistance. The ﬂuid inlet of the actuator is connected to
a terminal that is supplied with hot or cold ﬂuids and the outlet
is connected to a terminal that dumps the used ﬂuid into a lower
pressure reservoir. Entire wet SMA actuator arrays have been
developed to control hand and ﬁnger movement [10] and could
be used to control other high degree-of-freedom mechanisms as
well.

As more biologically inspired mechanisms are developed us-
ing wet SMA, it is necessary to develop ways of making these
robots self-sustaining (i.e., untethered). One step toward en-
abling these wet SMA robots is the development of an onboard
pump that can provide heating and cooling to sustain the actu-
ation of external subsystems using wet SMA technology. Just
as the wet SMA actuators behave like muscles with a cardio-
vascular system, a pump using wet SMA actuators would be
analogous to a heart.

blocks.text:
While this is the ﬁrst SMA device to use its own thermoﬂuidic
output to help sustain self-actuation, it is not the ﬁrst SMA pump.
Multiple microscale SMA pumps have been developed for de-
livering small amounts of ﬂuid for various MEMS-based chem-
ical delivery systems. One thin-ﬁlm SMA diaphragm pump is
capable of providing 50 μL/min [13]. Another novel recipro-
cating peristaltic pump prototype is capable of outputs up to
1000 μL/min of ﬂuid using SMA springs [14]. These electrically
heated and passively cooled SMA pumps are feasible on the mi-
croscale because the time constants with unforced convection
are much faster at the microscale. Since the robotic pump must
be able to actuate external wet SMA systems on a macroscale,
high net volume outputs on the order of mL/min are necessary.
To make these SMA pumps feasible at the macroscale, we can
take advantage of the forced-convection principles employed
in previous work [9], as well as novel bioinspiration from the
human heart.

blocks.text:
This paper presents the design, theoretical analysis, and
implementation of a biologically inspired wet SMA actuated
robotic pump that can distribute thermal energy via forced ﬂuid
convection to external wet SMA subsystems on a macroscale
over prolonged periods of time. The SMA pump uniquely draws
from its own thermoﬂuidic output to assist in actuating its own
internal SMA actuators. Simulations and experiments are used
to characterize the performance of the pump, and to demonstrate
that it can operate in a self-sustaining cycle with a net positive
output that is orders of magnitude larger than other SMA pumps.

blocks.text:
Since the SMA pump has to be able to provide both hot and
cold ﬂuids to other subsystems, there are two separate pumping
systems. Each pump system is comprised of an accumulator, a
reservoir, a pumping chamber, and a wet SMA actuator. The
accumulators provide the pressure necessary to force the ﬂuids
through the tubing and across the SMA actuators attached to a
lever, which is attached to the pumping chambers. The reservoirs
hold the ﬂuids after they have passed through the actuators. The
pumping chambers draw the ﬂuid from the reservoirs and pump
it back to the accumulators with the aid of check valves to
ensure unidirectional ﬂow. A set of timed valves control the
routing manifold to send alternating hot and cold ﬂuid to the
actuators. After the hot and cold ﬂuids are passed through the
actuators, a similar manifold is used to separate the exiting
hot and cold ﬂuids into their respective reservoirs. The timing
of the valves could be replaced with a mechanically parasitic
valve mechanism, much like the cam-valve mechanism in an
automobile engine.

and vice versa. This allows for variation in accumulator pressure
while still being able to cause some displacement in the pump-
ing chambers. This arrangement also requires that the hot and
cold chambers pump 180◦out of phase to avoid any unwanted
additional tension on the SMA actuators.

blocks.text: III. FEASIBILITY STUDY

lines.text: III. FEASIBILITY STUDY

blocks.text:
A feasibility study of the robotic pump system involves the
analysis of the net volumetric output in terms of output-to-
input ratio. Seven parameters largely inﬂuence this output per-
formance: SMA wire diameter, inner tube diameter, actuator
length, accumulator pressure, pumping chamber cross-sectional
area, mechanical advantage, and ﬂow duration. For example,
the diameter of the SMA wire affects the performance such that
larger diameter wires allow for higher force generation, but at
the cost of a lower rate of wire temperature change and, thus,
slower contraction. The inner tube diameter of the actuator also
affects the rate of temperature change of the SMA wire. How-
ever, increasing the tube diameter also increases the volumetric
input required into the system. Similarly, longer actuator lengths
require higher input volumes, but also provide larger strokes in
the pumping chambers, thus, increasing the volumetric output
of the robotic pump.

blocks.text:
The operating accumulator pressure affects the performance
in many ways. A higher accumulator pressure will lead to an in-
crease in ﬂow rate through the actuator and decrease in the actu-
ation time, but will also impose a stronger opposing force to the
actuators and output pumping chambers. Increasing the cross-
sectional area of the pumping chambers only compounds this
problem, but also increases the potential output of the system.
This can be somewhat alleviated by way of using mechanical
advantage through a lever.

blocks.text: IV. DYNAMIC MODELING AND SIMULATION

lines.text: IV. DYNAMIC MODELING AND SIMULATION

blocks.text:
It is beneﬁcial to model the SMA pump dynamics in order
to predict the behavior of the system under various conditions.
This helps alleviate the number of experiments required in order
to ﬁnd the set of parameters that yields optimal output perfor-
mance. In order to model the entire pump system, dynamic
models of both the SMA actuators and the rest of the system are
required. A modiﬁed version of the dynamic model derived by
Ertel and Mascaro [11], [18] will be used for this application.
Modiﬁcations to the model include the use of a differential hys-
teresis model of the SMA actuators [19], temperature-dependent
ﬂuid properties, the ability to use complex timing schemes, and
the ability to apply Joule heating to the SMA actuators.

lines.text: It is beneﬁcial to model the SMA pump dynamics in order
to predict the behavior of the system under various conditions.
This helps alleviate the number of experiments required in order
to ﬁnd the set of parameters that yields optimal output perfor-
mance. In order to model the entire pump system, dynamic
models of both the SMA actuators and the rest of the system are
required. A modiﬁed version of the dynamic model derived by
Ertel and Mascaro [11], [18] will be used for this application.
Modiﬁcations to the model include the use of a differential hys-
teresis model of the SMA actuators [19], temperature-dependent
ﬂuid properties, the ability to use complex timing schemes, and
the ability to apply Joule heating to the SMA actuators.

Ertel and Mascaro’s dynamic model was derived using energy
bond graphs and state-space methods. This allowed for combin-
ing individual wet SMA actuator models with the pumping sys-
tem model. Fig. 4 shows the complete bond graph used to derive
the state equations. In this ﬁgure, the actuators are divided into
three segments per actuator as opposed to 20 segments used in
the actual model. This bond graph couples two opposing actu-
ators each of which are attached to its own pumping chamber
through a lever with a given mechanical advantage. The effort
sources Se are martensite fractions modulated by SMA wire
temperature. These temperatures, determined by simulation of
hot and cold water passing through the wet SMA actuators, will
now be discussed.

While using longer actuators can be advantageous for larger
pump stroke, more ﬂow input is required and the heat loss to
the environment is increased. Due to this tradeoff, an optimal
actuator length is expected for peak performance. Similarly, a
high mechanical advantage can be beneﬁcial for overpowering
the accumulator pressure, but in a trade for decreased pump
stroke. Fig. 5 provides simulation results of output-to-input ratio
for varying actuator lengths and mechanical advantages.

blocks.text:
Flow durations of 4 s with a stagnation periods of 2 s were
used for actuation timing over two complete cycles. The ﬁgure
suggests that the performance of the pump is expected to reach
its maximum potential with actuator lengths between 35 and
45 cm. Also, as the mechanical advantage decreases, the output
increases for nearly all actuator lengths. Similar trends hold
true for other ﬂow durations as well. A mechanical advantage of
0.84 will be used for the remaining simulations since modeling
suggests that this conﬁguration produces the highest volume
output. Simulations using lower mechanical advantages suggest
higher outputs, but also indicate that the tensile stress in the
actuators may exceed the pulling strength of the SMA.

The ﬂow duration of the ﬂuid passing through the actuators
is critical to the performance of the pump. The optimal timing
will depend greatly on the actuator length. Longer actuators will
require longer ﬂow durations in order to cause full phase trans-
formation along the entire wire within the actuator while smaller
actuators will require less. In order to fully understand the re-
lationship between actuator length, ﬂow duration, and output
performance, multiple simulations need to be completed.

blocks.text:
The data presented in the ﬁgure suggest that ﬂow durations
between 1.5 and 2.0 s with little or no lead time yield the highest
overall performance. This seems intuitive since additional ﬂow
may be unnecessary with the electrical actuation. The data also
suggest that there is a point at which ﬂow duration is too small
since the ﬂuid propagation time through a 40-cm actuator is
roughly only 0.8 s. This is because the electrical actuation does
not provide enough heat to contract the SMA actuators with
colder ﬂuid surrounding them. The only way to compensate for
this effect would be to increase the amount of current being
passed through the SMA actuators. This would require more
capable power supplies to accommodate currents above 5 A.

to Fig. 4. As predicted, using a mechanical advantage of 0.84
yielded the best output results for all actuator lengths.

blocks.text: C. Heat Addition

lines.text: C. Heat Addition

blocks.text:
Without continuous heat addition to the system, the perfor-
mance of the pump degrades over time. Conversely, with heat
input, the performance is expected to be sustained and even ex-
ceed that of the nonheated system. This is because the boiling
point of the water will be higher due to the increased pressure
within the accumulators. An experimental comparison of the
output-to-input ratio over time using ﬂuid-only and electrical
actuation with 40-cm actuators with and without heat addition
is provided in Figs. 12 and 13, respectively. The results in the
ﬁgures conﬁrm that performance is sustained and that the per-
formance is signiﬁcantly higher with continuous heat addition
than without.

blocks.text: VI. CONCLUSION

lines.text: VI. CONCLUSION

blocks.text:
A biologically inspired wet SMA robotic pump has been cre-
ated that can provide thermal energy via ﬂuidic convection to
external wet SMA subsystems. The robotic pump uses its own
thermoﬂuidic output to assist in actuation of its own internal
SMA actuators similar to a heart. It has been shown by sim-
ulation and experimentation that the SMA pump is capable of
providing sufﬁcient amounts of ﬂuid to actuate external SMA
systems on a macroscale. This is evident by the volumetric
output-to-input ratios of 1.4 using ﬂuid-only actuation and 2.1
with the assistance of Joule heating. The pump is capable of
pumping a net output of 66 mL/min, which is two orders of
magnitude larger than any other SMA pump. This output can
be increased, as suggested in (10), by increasing the number of
contracting actuators.

blocks.text:
Future improvements planned for the robotic pump include
making the system more compact in volume, removing the need
for auxiliary electric inputs, and optimizing the practical efﬁ-
ciency of the pump. Making the system more compact while
maintaining a comparable volumetric output would require a
creative use of space while taking care not to impair the con-
traction of the SMA actuators. Methods to decrease the electrical
dependence include using ﬂuid-only heating and using mechan-
ically timed valves.

blocks.text:
As mentioned previously, the maximum theoretical efﬁciency
that this system can achieve is 3.4%. The actual efﬁciency of this
prototype system is much less, but the goal at this stage was not
to optimize efﬁciency but rather to ﬁrst demonstrate that a net
positive volumetric output was practically achievable. In future
work, we will seek to characterize and optimize the practical
efﬁciency of the system by minimizing thermal and mechanical
losses. The efﬁciency of the optimized system will still be much
lower than a pump driven by electric motors. However, this
efﬁciency disadvantage is theoretically offset by a 100 to 1
advantage in chemical versus electric energy storage. The SMA
pump also has the unique advantage of silent operation, which
may be important for certain applications. In theory, the SMA
pump could operate continuously and silently with only a high-
energy-density chemical energy source to keep the hot ﬂuid hot.

通过单轴拉伸试验研究了CuAlBe-SMA 缆索在循环
载荷作用下的力学特性，并在此基础上提出了一种
二维模型对其最大应力、残余应变、等效弹性模量
和等效粘性阻尼等进行预测。REEDLUNN 等[11-12]

lines.text: 通过单轴拉伸试验研究了CuAlBe-SMA 缆索在循环
载荷作用下的力学特性，并在此基础上提出了一种
二维模型对其最大应力、残余应变、等效弹性模量
和等效粘性阻尼等进行预测。REEDLUNN 等[11-12]

blocks.text:
通过一系列单轴拉伸试验研究了7×7 和1×27 两种
不同缠绕方式的NiTi-SMA 缆索在室温下的超弹性
行为，并与NiTi-SMA 丝的拉伸力学行为进行对比
表明，7×7 结构的NiTi-SMA 缆索在应力诱发相变
过程中具有明显的相变峰值及相变平台特征，且相
较于1×7 芯股，7×7 缆索的相变应力平台有所降低。
OZBULUT 等[13]和SHERIF 等[14]通过单轴拉伸和循
环加载试验研究了加载率和应变幅值对NiTi-SMA
超弹性缆索在变形过程中应力-应变场和温度场的
影响及其低周疲劳特性。MAS 等[15]通过试验研究了
NiTi-SMA 缆索在不同温度和不同加载率下的超弹
性响应以及循环疲劳特性，通过粘结试验研究了
NiTi-SMA 缆索与混凝土之间的粘结效应，为
NiTi-SMA 缆索增强混凝土的实际应用提供了试验
基础。CARBONI 等[16]通过理论分析建立了SMA 缆
索的现象学模型并与试验结果进行了对比验证。 
ZHENG等[17]将SMA缆索用于一种智能桥梁的轴承
设计中，并提出一种针对其弹性恢复和循环加载疲
劳寿命的评价方法。

blocks.text: Nonlinear Vibration Absorber with Pinched Hysteresis:

lines.text: Nonlinear Vibration Absorber with Pinched Hysteresis:

blocks.text: Theory and Experiments

lines.text: Theory and Experiments

blocks.text: Biagio Carboni1 and Walter Lacarbonara2

lines.text: Biagio Carboni1 and Walter Lacarbonara2

blocks.text:
Abstract: A nonlinear vibration absorber exploiting the pinched hysteresis of mixed wire ropes made of NiTiNOL and steel is proposed.
The mixed wire ropes are assembled in a mechanical device which, by bending them, provides the restoring force to the oscillating mass. The
assembly of mixed wire ropes, subject to cyclic end displacements, gives rise to a pinched force-displacement behavior due to the simulta-
neous occurrence of interwire friction and phase transformations. A modified Bouc-Wen model is adopted to represent the pinched hysteresis
while the differential evolutionary (DE) algorithm is employed to identify the constitutive parameters that reproduce the experimental force-
displacement cycles. The DE algorithm is also utilized to optimize the restoring force of the absorber toward mitigation of the dynamic
response of the main structure to external disturbances of various magnitudes. The pinched hysteresis provides an equivalent damping ratio
and resonance frequency, which tend to become almost constant in a given oscillation amplitude range, thus overcoming detrimental detuning
problems typical of other nonlinear absorbers. The absorber performance is evaluated in the context of a multistory steel building model
mounted on a shaking table. The comparison between controlled and uncontrolled responses shows a very good attenuation performance
within the design frequency bandwidth. DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)EM.1943-7889.0001072. © 2016 American Society of Civil Engineers.

blocks.text: Introduction

lines.text: Introduction

blocks.text:
Mitigation of the dynamic response of structures subject to excita-
tions is often based on the use of so-called vibration absorbers, also
known as tuned mass dampers (TMDs). A TMD has the role of
applying control forces to the main structure that can introduce pos-
itive damping to reduce the oscillation amplitude. This approach
can be successful in ensuring safety and comfort for structures
in which the architectural requirements are reflected into slender-
ness and, thus flexibility and low damping. Typical civil structures
characterized by high slenderness and low damping are long-span
bridges, footbridges, tall buildings, and skyscrapers. TMDs can be
effective in reducing oscillations caused either by narrow-band
excitations such as wind or by broadband excitations such as
earthquakes.

blocks.text:
The extension of the theory to damped SDOF systems for differ-
ent loading conditions has been investigated by numerous research-
ers. Significant contributions were made by Randall et al. (1981),
Warburton (1982), Warburton and Ayorinde (1980), and Tsai and
Lin (1993). Ioi and Ikeda (1978) proposed empirical design formu-
las relating the tuning frequency and the optimal damping of the
absorber to the mass ratio (i.e., ratio between the TMD mass
and the main mass).

blocks.text:
The disadvantages of the linearly damped TMDs led many re-
searchers to investigate nonlinear designs. Inaudi and Kelly (1995)
studied a TMD based on a friction device acting transversely to the
motion. The benefits of this device consist in a lower sensitivity to
temperature changes and an easy adjustment to the desired param-
eters. The main limitation is that the optimization depends on the
excitation level, thus requiring an accurate estimate of the excita-
tion forces. Lim et al. (2006) investigated a hardening Duffing os-
cillator subject to harmonic excitations. Lacarbonara and Vestroni
(2002) proposed the concept of a hysteretic TMD and analyzed its
feasibility in the case of low-rise multistory buildings. Attractive
semiactive TMDs are based on magneto-rheological fluids whose
viscosity can be varied applying a magnetic field to the fluid
(Carlson et al. 1996).

Wire ropes are typically employed to resist large loads thanks
to the funicular load-bearing mechanism. In the last century, the
idea of exploiting the complicated mechanical behavior of wire
ropes to dissipate and absorb energy became popular. When a short
wire rope is forced to deform, a relative motion and therefore fric-
tion between individual wires takes place, thereby dissipating en-
ergy. Stockbridge [“Vibration damper,” US Patent No. US1675391
A (1928)] presented a damper based on the interwire friction in
strands with two oscillating masses whose support is fixed onto
power lines to reduce wind-induced vibrations. Wire ropes were
also used in the vibration isolation of devices that control the
passage of fluid to rocket engines (Tinker and Cutchins 1992).
Demetriades et al. (1993) used wire rope springs in seismic protec-
tion of sensitive equipment in buildings. Gerges and Vickery (2003,
2005) studied experimentally the performance of a class of TMDs
which rely on wire rope springs. Carpineto et al. (2014) and
Vestroni et al. patented [“Hysteretic tuned mass damper for
passive control of mechanical vibration,” Italian Patent No.
RM2011A000434 (2011)] a vibration absorber (VA) based on
the hysteretic restoring force of short clamped-clamped steel ropes
subject to flexural cycles. They showed good performance of the
device in reducing the oscillation amplitude of a simply-supported
beam subject to harmonic and transient dynamical loads.

ploit the pinched hysteretic restoring force provided by an assembly
of mixed NiTiNOL-steel wire ropes subject to flexural cycles. The
absorber is an evolution of the rheological device presented in
Carboni et al. (2015). The device is capable of providing different
kinds of hysteretic behavior changing the arrangements of

description of the hysteresis loops was achieved introducing a

1976) and employing the differential evolutionary (DE) algorithm
(Storn and Price 1997) for the model parameters identification.

blocks.text:
vibrations,” European Patent Application No. 12773392.1 (2015)]
is employed in one of its operating modes with an assembly of
mixed wire ropes made of NiTiNOL and stainless steel. This
assembly provides quasi-linear-softening force-displacement cycles
with a pinching at the origin. The pinched behavior is due to the
occurrence of interwire friction and martensitic phase transforma-
tions in the shape memory material. In this paper, the optimization
is performed considering a 2DOF system constituted by the princi-
pal mass to which the absorber mass is attached by means of a quasi-
linear-softening pinched (QSP) restoring force. The optimization
process selects the most suitable QSP hysteresis cycles for mitigat-
ing structural oscillations induced by external disturbances. The
QSP restoring force provides an equivalent damping ratio and
resonance frequency that become nearly constant in a given oscil-
lation amplitude range. These features overcome the detrimental
detuning effects exhibited by other nonlinear hysteretic TMDs.
The performance of the QSP vibration absorber mounted on the
top floor of a multistory steel building scale model is tested using
a shaking table. The uncontrolled response is compared with the
controlled response considering several base excitation levels rang-
ing from soft to hard excitations.

blocks.text: NiTiNOL-Steel Wire Ropes and the Absorber

lines.text: NiTiNOL-Steel Wire Ropes and the Absorber

blocks.text:
The idea of combining stainless steel and NiTiNOL wires in the
manufacturing of a new wire rope is due to different reasons.
The first stems from the objective of obtaining a cost-effective wire
rope capable of dissipating a great amount of energy without ex-
hibiting inelastic stains. A second aspect is associated with the fact
that the steel wires placed in the external layers facilitate the manu-
facturing process while improving the stability of the rope in con-
sideration of the strong elasticity of the shape memory material.
Finally, the type of steel and shape memory wires and their relative
positions in the wire rope formation can be designed to give rise to
particular constitutive behaviors under tension and bending.

blocks.text:
The proposed TMD features the restoring force provided by an
assembly of short wire ropes subject to flexural cycles. The wire
rope has been designed and manufactured using both NITiNOL
and stainless steel wires. The NiTiNOL behaves as a superelastic
alloy at the ambient temperature around the 20°C. The starting aus-
tenite transformation temperature is about −25°C. The wire rope is
single-stranded with 61 wires arranged in layers of different mate-
rials. All wires have a diameter of 0.63 mm and the rope presents a
global diameter of 5.7 mm. The wire rope was manufactured by
In.tra.Flex (Oggiono, Italy) using the design provided by the au-
thors. The manufacturing process offers challenging aspects due
to the strong shape-recovery capacity. The position of the NiTiNOL
layers is optimized against the bending loads acting on the wire
ropes. Fig. 1 shows the 61-wire rope. Hereafter, the mixed-wire
rope will be denoted by NiTi-ST61.

The identification of the material parameters using the experi-
mental measurements is carried out by employing the DE algo-
rithm. This is a heuristic method suitable for discontinuous and
strongly nonlinear optimization problems since there are no restric-
tions on the cost function. For each parameter to identify, a range of

parameters is assembled selecting for each parameter a set of values
drawn from a Gaussian distribution in the range of variation. The
vectors are combined with simple algebraic formulas and with the
crossover operation, typical of genetic algorithms, and a new im-
proved population is found selecting parameter values that mini-
mize the cost function. In the present case, the cost function is
the mean-square error (MSE). Denoting by fðxÞ and ˆfðxÞ the ex-
perimentally measured force and the model-based restoring force

The results for configuration S2b are shown in Fig. 4. For each
amplitude, 10 experimental cycles are obtained, out of which one of
the stabilized cycles is extracted and identified. The number of vec-
tors forming the population of the DE algorithm is 40 while the
number of iterations is 150. The restoring force exhibits a quasi-
linear trend at low amplitudes while at high amplitudes a pinching
effect is observed. This is due to the interplay between the interwire
friction and the NiTiNOL phase transformations. At high ampli-
tudes during the loading process, the phase transformations occur
in the NiTiNOL layers, determining an increment of the dissipated
energy. The identification is performed employing the extended
BW model and very good results are obtained with 150 iterations
of the DE. Table 1 shows the parameters identified for the hyste-
resis cycles and the related MSEs.

blocks.text:
For a full characterization of the nonlinear dynamic behavior,
path following of the periodic response upon variation of some
of the forcing parameters is carried out. In particular, this study
examined frequency-response curves for fixed ground acceleration
magnitudes. To this end, a continuation procedure based on the
Jacobian of the Poincaré Map is adopted in the case of the non-
linear oscillator characterized by the QSP material behavior. The
adopted computational method (Lacarbonara and Vestroni 2003;
Lacarbonara 2013) is a pseudo-arc-length method. This procedure
is based on a sequential application of the Newton-Raphson
method on an augmented system of equations. It is based on an
adjoint orthogonality condition through which the solution at the
next step is searched along the normal to the tangent vector in
the current solution point. A full description of this method can
be found in Lacarbonara (2013).

blocks.text:
The main advantage of the implemented path-following method
based on the Poincaré Map lies in the fact that the procedure, by
which the Jacobian of the map and the derivative of the map with
respect to the control parameter are computed via finite differences,
furnishes the monodromy matrix as a by-product of the continu-
ation from which the stability of the periodic solutions can be as-
certained. In the present case, the control parameter coincides with
the nondimensional excitation frequency ~Ω and the Poincaré Map
is evaluated with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme
over an interval equal to the excitation period. The algorithm is
implemented in MATLAB.

The FRCs of the device in configuration S2b for increasing exci-

tests on a shaking table. The frame F1 of the device is fixed on
the shaking table by means of four supports while bar B1 of frame
F2 lies on four ball bearings by means of a steel plate. The ball
bearings can slide on two cylindrical shafts, which have their ends
fixed on frame F1. Thus, the frame F2 can translate relative to F1
and acts as the oscillating mass. A displacement transducer
(Hottinger Baldwin Messtechnik GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany) and
an accelerometer (PCB Piezotronics, Depew, New York) measure

blocks.text:
The experimental FRCs are reported in Fig. 8. Figs. 9(a and b)
show the periodic solution at the resonance frequency and the am-
plitude of the associated Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) in logarith-
mic scale, respectively. The softening behavior is confirmed and the
numerical prediction regarding the saturated resonance frequency is
correct. However, there is a mismatch in terms of the levels of base
acceleration for which the same displacement amplitudes of the
TMD are achieved in the numerical and experimental simulations.
The experimental base acceleration amplitudes are larger. The vis-
cous damping, the additional friction on the shaft guides, and the
limitation inherent in the use of a single set of material parameters
in the computations play an important role. These are identified as
the causes of the quantitative differences between the numerical
and the experimental results. New parameter sets that can better
fit the experimental FRCs are evaluated employing the DE algo-
rithm. The same DE algorithm as used before for the hysteresis
cycles’ identification is adopted. The only difference is that now
the MSE is computed using the experimental and numerical FRCs.
The comparison between the experimentally obtained and the nu-
merically identified FRCs is shown in Fig. 10. The response curves
obtained for low excitation levels are better identified. In particular,
the numerical branches to the right side of the resonance frequency
are closer to the experimental responses. Table 2 gives the param-
eters through the identification of the experimental FRCs. These
parameters are then used to compute the numerical FRCs in Fig. 10.
The restoring force has the form:f ¼ kex þ z where the hysteretic
force z is that of the modified BW model [Eq. (2)] illustrated in
section “Hysteresis of NiTiNOL-Steel Wire Ropes and Phenom-
enological Identification.”

The optimization of the nonlinear hysteretic TMD to be sought
in the space of the absorber material parameters depends on the
excitation level, since the stiffness and damping of a nonlinear os-
cillator vary with the oscillation amplitude. A typical approach
to the optimization of an hysteretic absorber resorts to using the
closed-form expressions for the frequency tuning and optimal
damping of the viscoelastic TMD considering the equivalent prop-
erties of the nonlinear absorber for a given oscillation amplitude. A
drawback of this approach is that a variation of the excitation am-
plitude can give rise to significant detuning from the optimal case.
The new idea proposed in this paper consists in using DE to opti-
mize the material parameters of the TMD for multiple excitation
amplitudes within a given range.

The main advantage of the proposed optimization method is that
the algorithm tends naturally to find a solution that best minimizes
the response for the highest excitation amplitude. This is due to the
fact that the larger contribution to the cost function is given by the
FRC for the higher excitation levels. A design of this type is par-
ticularly suitable in ensuring that the ultimate limit state is not
reached. However, if the TMD design is tuned towards the service-
ability limit state, different weights can be introduced to give
greater importance to the responses to low excitation levels.

The optimization of the hysteretic TMD is performed consider-
ing the nondimensional system described by Eqs. (21)–(24). The
mass ratio μ is assumed equal to 0.1 while the structure damping
ratio ξ0 is equal to 1%. The nondimensional frequency range of the
base excitation is [0.87, 1.14]. Three different levels of base exci-
tation are considered evaluating four sets of optimal material
parameters. A set is optimized to control the response of the system
for all three excitation levels while the other optimizations are per-
formed to control each individual level of base motion. The three
base excitation levels are referred to as low, medium, and high. The
parameters set optimized to control all levels of base excitation is
denoted by Hyst-all while the parameters sets optimized to control
the low, medium and high levels of base excitation are denoted by
Hyst-low, Hyst-med, and Hyst-high, respectively. The performance
of the hysteretic TMD is compared with that of the linear absorber
optimized with the empirical Ioi-Ikeda formulas (Ioi and Ikeda
1978). The optimal frequency ratio (i.e., ratio between the fre-
quency of the TMD and that of the main structure) is fopt ¼ 0.993
while the optimal damping ratio of the absorber is ξs ¼ 6.23%.

Fig. 12(a) shows the FRCs for the medium excitation level. The
Hyst-all case approaches the optimal condition with the two peaks
being almost equal. The three curves are very close, but the re-
sponse of the Hyst-med TMD is slightly lower than that of the linear
absorber except for the peak amplitude at a frequency near 0.93,
where it exceeds the other responses. In Fig. 12(b) the frequency
responses of the TMDs are shown. For the frequency band centered
about the main system resonance, the response of Hyst-med is the
greatest followed by Hyst-all and the linear absorber. Away from
the resonance frequency, there is a crossover of the curve associated
to the linear device, beyond which it becomes higher than the other.
This is due to the fact that the hysteretic device has a high damping
ratio for small amplitudes. Figs. 12(c and d) represent the hysteretic
cycles for the Hyst-all and Hyst-med optimization, respectively.
The Hyst-all force-displacement curves present a pinching about
the origin in contrast with the Hyst-med optimization. For the
low excitation level, the oscillation amplitude is small enough that
the pinching behavior is not manifested. The same occurs for the
optimization Hyst-low where the DE algorithm seeks to find a con-
stitutive configuration with low damping for small amplitudes.
Thus, the parameters ξ and yc take values such that the area
enclosed by the force-displacement cycles gets reduced.

blocks.text:
detunings caused by to the significant variations of the frequency
and damping with the oscillation amplitude play the most important
role in the design of hysteretic absorbers. The approach presented
in this paper has attempted to overcome this limitation by using the
pinched hysteresis exhibited by the mixed NiTiNOL-steel wire
rope under flexure and by adopting a new optimization strategy
that allows the design process to include a range of working oscil-
lation amplitudes corresponding to a range of excitation magni-
tudes. As shown in Fig. 14, when the DE method is used to
optimize the hysteretic absorber for a single excitation level, the
constitutive behaviors selected by the algorithm are such that
the optimal damping is achieved for the displacement amplitude
exhibited by the absorber at the main system resonance frequency.
Therefore a force-displacement cycle without pinching, typical of
short steel wire ropes subject to bending, is obtained. The optimi-
zation carried out accounting for a range of excitation amplitudes
provides a constitutive behavior such that the associated damping,
after reaching a peak within a tiny range of displacements, becomes
nearly constant over a fairly large range of higher displacements.
This behavior is given by the pinched force-displacement cycles
that can be obtained with the assembly of mixed NiTiNOL-steel
wire ropes under flexure. When the phase transformations occur
in the shape memory material due to high bending curvatures of
the wire ropes, the energy dissipation increases and compensates
for the typical roll off of the ratio between dissipated energy
and elastic stored energy which, instead, remains constant.

blocks.text:
Experimental Validation on a Multistory Steel
Building

lines.text: Experimental Validation on a Multistory Steel
Building

blocks.text:
The results and the methodologies presented in preceding sections
are applied to an experimental case study. The developed TMD
prototype is optimized to mitigate the dynamic response of a re-
duced scale multistory building subject to unidirectional shaking
table tests. The main target is the mitigation of the resonant
dynamic response dominated by the fundamental mode of the
structure. The modal properties are first identified on the basis
of free-vibration tests, hammer-blow tests, and experimental FRCs
assuming a shear-type model for the building. The TMD constit-
utive properties are optimized employing the procedure described
in section “Differential Evolutionary Optimization of the Restoring
Force toward Vibration Absorption” whereby the shear-type
MDOF building model was reduced to a SDOF oscillator incorpo-
rating the features of the identified first mode. The wire ropes’ ar-
rangement, which provides the optimal constitutive behavior of the
absorber, is obtained with a further experimental campaign that
makes use of the MTS testing machine and employing, as starting
point, the force-displacement curves of the presented configuration
S2b. Experimentally obtained FRCs for different base excitation
levels are evaluated for the controlled and uncontrolled building.

60 mm and thickness of 5 mm. The building is supported by four
columns placed at the corners of the floors thus forming with the
beams a spatial frame comprising two planar frames in each
orthogonal direction. The clamped connections between the beams
and the columns are obtained by means of flanged joints. The
beams ends are welded to steel plates which, in turn, are bolted
onto the columns. The bottom ends of the columns are welded onto
thick steel plates, which are bolted on the shaking table. These base
joints are made stiffer by welding four trapezoidal steel plates be-
tween each column bottom end and the connecting foundation
plates. The scaled building prototype can be considered a mo-
ment-resisting frame (MRF). The floors are reinforced concrete
(RC) slabs with a thickness of about 4 cm and are connected to
the steel beams by a number of bolts. The presence of the RC slabs
delivers high stiffness to the floors in the horizontal direction, thus
providing a shear-type behavior to the building model. The steel
L-shaped columns (i.e., without reinforcements) have a low
torsional stiffness, leading to the fact that the frequency of the tor-
sional mode would be very close to the frequency of the lowest
translational mode (i.e., along the wider floor side). For this reason,
the profiles are stiffened against torsional rotations by welding
two triangular plates between the angles of the columns at every
joint with the beams. The steel constituting the L-shaped profiles
and the concrete rebars have characteristic tensile strengths equal
to ftk ¼ 235 and ftk ¼ 450 MPa, respectively. The characteristic

The total mass of the building is 677 kg, of which 203.27 kg is
structural mass due to the columns, beams, plates, and bolts while
the remaining part is the mass of the concrete slabs. The latter do
not have exactly the same mass, which from the first to the last
floor, is equal to 101.45, 99.7, 99.175, 83.7, and 89.75 kg, respec-
tively. On the fifth floor, the masses of the TMD frame and the four
supports represent additional masses equal to 16.64 and 21.4 kg,
respectively. The TMD rectangular frame and the supports re-
present the necessary infrastructure that hosts the TMD oscillating
mass on the top floor of the building. Thus, their masses must be
considered as mass of the building. In order to evaluate the mass
that can be assigned to each individual floor, the structural mass is
divided proportionally considering the associated influence areas.
Table 4 shows the mass attributed to each floor of the building.

are performed by assigning initial conditions in two different ways.
First, small displacements are prescribed, pulling and releasing the
beams of the top floor. In this case, the acceleration signals are used
to compute the natural frequencies through the FFT. In order to
evaluate the lowest frequency associated with the rotational mode,
two accelerometers are placed on the diagonal opposite ends of the
fifth floor long beams, and the building is pulled and released from
a long beam end that does not have an accelerometer mounted.
Fig. 17 demonstrates the free-vibration tests. Considering the fact
that the positive accelerations measured by Accelerometer 1 are
negative for Accelerometer 2 [Fig. 17(c)] summing the two re-
corded signals the translational component becomes close to zero
while the rotational component is acquired. Hence, by evaluating
the resulting signals in the frequency domain, it is possible to
obtain the natural frequency associated with the rotational mode.
Figs. 18(a and b) show the FFTs of the top floor free-vibration re-
sponse in terms of acceleration in the long and short building di-
rections, respectively. Fig. 18(c) contains the FFT of the signal
obtained by summing the response recorded by Accelerometers
1 and 2 [Fig. 17(c)]. The natural frequencies associated with the
translational and rotational modes are 4.23 Hz (sway mode in
the long direction), 4.45 Hz (sway mode in the short direction),
and 7 Hz (twist mode).

associated with the two translational sway modes and to the rota-

damping ratio increases. This behavior is well documented in
the technical literature, especially for towers and high-rise build-
ings (Jeary 1986; Tamura et al. 1993; Tamura and Suganuma
1996; Fang et al. 1999).

blocks.text:
The main finding regarding the optimization of the nonlinear
absorber against different excitation levels consists in making
the device work in the displacement range in which it exhibits al-
most constant values of the resonance frequency and damping ratio.
This strategy, which has a clear physical interpretation, has been
suggested by the DE algorithm selecting a hysteresis shape that
assumes values of the resonance frequency and damping very close
to the optimal values of the linear viscoelastic absorber in a large
displacement interval. The optimal values of the resonance fre-
quency and damping ratio of a linear viscoelastic absorber com-
puted with the Ioi-Ikeda empirical formulas are 4.014 Hz and
6.71%, respectively. In Fig. 23(a) the FRCs of the hysteretic
absorber are shown for increasing levels of base excitation together
with the optimal resonance frequency of the linear viscoelastic
absorber represented by the black dotted line. Above a certain
oscillation amplitude, the hysteretic device exhibits a resonance
frequency almost constant and equal to the optimal resonance fre-
quency of the linear absorber. In Fig. 23(b), the trend of the equiv-
alent damping ratio is shown as a function of the displacement
amplitude. The optimal displacement range in which the nonlinear
absorber achieves the best performance is past the peak where it
attains an almost constant damping ratio close to the optimal damp-
ing ratio of the linear viscoelastic absorber (black dotted line).

blocks.text:
Configuration S2c provides a constitutive behavior very similar
to that found by the optimization. However, this optimal behavior is
obtained performing quasi-static tests with the device mounted in
the vertical position under the MTS (Fig. 2). When the device is
mounted on the building, four ball bearings are fixed to the oscil-
lating mass in order to sustain its weight yet allowing horizontal
motion. This mechanism determines an additional damping of
the system and the dynamical force-displacement cycles present
a higher amount of dissipated energy with respect to the static case.
This effect has been already assessed in the dynamical tests with the
vibration absorber on the shaking table.

blocks.text:
The scale model building is subject to harmonic tests carried out
using the shaking table in the Department of Structural and
Geotechnical Engineering Laboratory. The tests are performed
on the uncontrolled and controlled buildings with the hysteretic
TMD (assembled according to the S2c configuration). The TMD
oscillating mass is 6.46 kg. Four different base acceleration levels
are considered, (0.023, 0.030, 0.038, and 0.045g). The acceleration
is maintained constant varying its frequency in the range [3.5,5] Hz
with an incremental step of 0.025 Hz. For each frequency step, a
sufficient number of excitation cycles are reached so as to obtain
steady-state oscillations of the building. The displacement of the
top floor is measured by a laser sensor (Micro-Epsilon Messtech-
nik, Ortenburg, Germany) and the relative displacement of the
oscillating mass with respect to the building is measured by an in-
ductive transducer
(Hottinger
Baldwin
Messtechnik
GmbH,
Darmstadt, Germany).

lines.text: Conclusions

blocks.text:
A new nonlinear vibration absorber based on the hysterisis of
NiTiNOL and steel wire ropes has been proposed (Carboni et al.
2015). To this end, new single-stranded mixed ropes constituted by
layers of NiTiNOL and steel wires were manufactured. The vibra-
tion absorber exploits the damping due to the interwire friction
and phase transformations together with a nonlinear mechanism
capable of inducing geometric nonlinearities. These features give
rise to a new rheological device that can operate according to four
different constitutive behaviors: quasi-linear-softening hysteresis,
quasi-linear-softening pinched hysteresis (QSP), strongly pinched
hardening hysteresis, and slightly pinched hardening hysteresis.

lines.text: A new nonlinear vibration absorber based on the hysterisis of
NiTiNOL and steel wire ropes has been proposed (Carboni et al.
2015). To this end, new single-stranded mixed ropes constituted by
layers of NiTiNOL and steel wires were manufactured. The vibra-
tion absorber exploits the damping due to the interwire friction
and phase transformations together with a nonlinear mechanism
capable of inducing geometric nonlinearities. These features give
rise to a new rheological device that can operate according to four
different constitutive behaviors: quasi-linear-softening hysteresis,
quasi-linear-softening pinched hysteresis (QSP), strongly pinched
hardening hysteresis, and slightly pinched hardening hysteresis.

blocks.text:
The pinched hysteresis has been described mathematically em-
ploying a modified version of the Bouc-Wen model. Moreover, the
identification of the material parameters, on the basis of the exper-
imental measurements, has been accurately performed by means of
a variant of the differential evolutionary algorithm.

lines.text: The pinched hysteresis has been described mathematically em-
ploying a modified version of the Bouc-Wen model. Moreover, the
identification of the material parameters, on the basis of the exper-
imental measurements, has been accurately performed by means of
a variant of the differential evolutionary algorithm.

blocks.text:
The hysteretic absorber has been characterized by computing
the frequency-response curves. The quasi-linear-softening pinched
restoring force has been found to exhibit a suitable behavior for
mitigating vibrations in the main structure. For increasing excita-
tion amplitudes, the absorber maintains a nearly constant resonance
frequency. Moreover, thanks to the phase transformations in the
NiTiNOL wires, the ratio between elastic and dissipated energy
is almost constant for a large displacement range. These dynamical
features have been observed experimentally through shaking table
tests of the TMD alone, thus validating the numerical predictions.

the frequency-response curves. The quasi-linear-softening pinched
restoring force has been found to exhibit a suitable behavior for
mitigating vibrations in the main structure. For increasing excita-
tion amplitudes, the absorber maintains a nearly constant resonance
frequency. Moreover, thanks to the phase transformations in the
NiTiNOL wires, the ratio between elastic and dissipated energy
is almost constant for a large displacement range. These dynamical
features have been observed experimentally through shaking table
tests of the TMD alone, thus validating the numerical predictions.

blocks.text:
The optimization of the TMD material properties for controlling
the resonant dynamics of a linear structure based on the DE
algorithm has shown that the QSP restoring force is the optimal
restoring force for mitigating vibrations caused by different
excitation levels. The consequence is that the typical detuning
phenomenon of other nonlinear hysteretic absorbers, due to the sen-
sitive dependence on the oscillation amplitude, can be overcome.

algorithm has shown that the QSP restoring force is the optimal
restoring force for mitigating vibrations caused by different

blocks.text:
A scaled multistory steel building has been adopted as case
study for validating experimentally the hysteretic TMD perfor-
mance. The constitutive behavior of the absorber has been
optimized to control the building’s oscillations dominated by its
lowest sway mode. Harmonic tests for different excitation ampli-
tudes in a frequency bandwidth centered about the sway mode have
been performed on the uncontrolled and controlled configurations.
The TMD characterized by the QSP hysteresis has shown very
good attenuation performance, reducing considerably the reso-
nance peaks for different excitation scenarios.

tudes in a frequency bandwidth centered about the sway mode have

nance peaks for different excitation scenarios.

blocks.text:
The advantage of the proposed hysteretic absorber over other
devices consists in it capability of providing different hysteresis
shapes according to the considered application. To control a
linear-elastic structure, the traditional linear vibration absorbers be-
have practically as linear systems only within a small displacement
range. On the contrary, the larger displacement range in which both
damping and stiffness are almost constant represents an optimal
range for the proposed nonlinear absorber.

blocks.text:
Abstract: The mechanical behaviors of laboratory-fabricated steel and superelastic shape memory
alloy (SMA) wire ropes are assessed in this study through a comprehensive approach encompassing
both experimental investigations and finite element (FE) numerical simulations. The assessment
of steel wire ropes involves experimental scrutiny under sinusoidal cyclic loading and natural
earthquake loading conditions. In parallel, SMA wire ropes’ behaviors are analyzed utilizing FE
simulations employing the widely acknowledged ABAQUS software version 2020. The validation of
all numerical simulations is undertaken against the experimentally observed behaviors. Moreover,
full-scale steel wire ropes are subjected to shaking table tests to validate the simulations, facilitating a
comparative analysis between the mechanical responses of SMA and steel wire ropes. The findings
demonstrate that SMA wire ropes exhibit superelastic behavior akin to SMA wires, with marginal

lines.text: Abstract: The mechanical behaviors of laboratory-fabricated steel and superelastic shape memory
alloy (SMA) wire ropes are assessed in this study through a comprehensive approach encompassing
both experimental investigations and finite element (FE) numerical simulations. The assessment
of steel wire ropes involves experimental scrutiny under sinusoidal cyclic loading and natural
earthquake loading conditions. In parallel, SMA wire ropes’ behaviors are analyzed utilizing FE
simulations employing the widely acknowledged ABAQUS software version 2020. The validation of
all numerical simulations is undertaken against the experimentally observed behaviors. Moreover,
full-scale steel wire ropes are subjected to shaking table tests to validate the simulations, facilitating a
comparative analysis between the mechanical responses of SMA and steel wire ropes. The findings
demonstrate that SMA wire ropes exhibit superelastic behavior akin to SMA wires, with marginal
variations in overall response observed across distinct configurations, akin to steel wire ropes.
Furthermore, augmenting the helix angle of SMA wire ropes results in reduced stress and increased
strain when exposed to the El Centro earthquake scenario. Nevertheless, the mechanical response of
SMA wire ropes closely mirrors that of a single wire.

blocks.text:
Cables are a type of structural element capable of resisting high tensile loads. They
are formed by twisting multiple wire strands together and are referred to as a “cable” if
the diameter is less than 3/8 inch or one centimeter, and “wire rope” if the diameter is
greater. Reverse lay cables have wires twisted in the opposite direction to the strands
in the cable, providing resistance to pressure and deformation but lower flexibility and
wear resistance. Lang lay cables have wires twisted in the same direction as the strands,
resulting in higher wear resistance. Cables have become increasingly important in civil
engineering, particularly in bridge construction [1,2]. Hosseinzadeh et al. [3] investigated
the utilization of cable braces to control lateral displacement and enhance bending frame
resistance. Shiravand et al. [4] studied the impact of cable rupture during earthquakes
and under uniform support excitation on the seismic response of cable-stayed bridges,
considering nonlinear behavior.

damping properties, dissipating energy during seismic events. The Martensite phase
induces the shape memory effect, enabling SMAs to recover their original shape upon
stimulation. The Austenite phase induces the superelastic effect, allowing SMAs to undergo
substantial deformations and revert to their original form when the stimulus is removed.
Both phenomena entail significant energy dissipation. Numerous studies have investigated
using SMAs for vibration control of civil structures. For example, Dolce et al. [5] examined
the advantageous characteristics of SMA-based isolation devices and systems for seismic
protection. They integrated the optimal mechanical traits of quasi-elastic and elastoplastic
devices, along with exceptional fatigue resistance and high corrosion resistance inherited
from NiTi-SMA. Han et al. [6] presented the energy dissipation principle of SMA wire
and developed an SMA damper device for structural control implementation. Corbi [7]
explored the advantages of SMA behavior in the dynamic response of structural systems.
They analyzed the impact of SMA tendons on the strength of an elastic-plastic structural
model subjected to horizontal shaking and vertical loads. McCormick et al. [8] utilized
superelastic NiTi shape memory alloy wires and bars to mitigate seismic vibrations in
buildings. Parulekar et al. [9] deliberated on the utilization of memory SMA dampers
fabricated from Austenite wires, particularly Nickel Titanium wires, for passive energy
absorption in earthquake engineering. Hu et al. [10] developed two innovative bracing
systems to enhance the seismic resilience of buildings. The Partially Self-Centering Brace
(PSB) combines NiTi-based SMA (NiTi-SMA) and iron-based SMA (Fe-SMA) U-shaped
dampers, where the NiTi-SMA provides self-centering capability and the Fe-SMA offers
energy dissipation, allowing flexible control of the self-centering function. In addition,
they [11] proposed the Hybrid Self-Centering Brace (HSB), which integrates NiTi-based
SMA U-shaped dampers and frequency-dependent viscoelastic dampers, with the SMA
dampers providing self-centering to avoid structural damage and the viscoelastic dampers
introducing velocity-proportional damping for nonstructural damage control. Both studies
concluded that these bracing systems have promising potential for enhancing the seismic
resilience of buildings. Although the cost of SMA components is higher than that of
traditional components, the latest investigations confirmed the life-cycle span benefits of
SMA-based braces with reduced initial costs [12]. Alternative configurations for SMA-based
superelasticity-assisted sliders (SSS) were proposed by Narjabadifam et al. [13].

SMA elements are frequently employed to manage vibrations in structures, but the
manufacturing of large-diameter SMA bars can be relatively expensive. As a result, the use
of SMA cables made up of smaller-diameter wires has become a more cost-effective alterna-
tive. For instance, a 6.35 mm diameter Nitinol bar can cost around $400 per meter, whereas
a comparable 49-wire Nitinol cable with a similar outer diameter of 7 × 7 × 0.711 mm is
significantly more affordable at only $60 per meter [14]. This substantial cost difference has
driven researchers to investigate the performance and applications of superelastic SMA
cables, which can provide the desired vibration control and energy dissipation capabilities
at a lower manufacturing cost compared to large solid SMA bars.

Existing research on SMA ropes has largely focused on basic tensile tests and the cyclic
loading of specific rope designs. However, for practical applications, especially in seismic
contexts, it is crucial to thoroughly examine their performance under earthquake conditions
through computer simulations, experimental studies, or both. SMA materials, especially in
wire rope form, offer promising structural applications due to their super-elastic properties.
Despite this potential, current studies have predominantly investigated the direct tension
or cyclic behavior of SMA cables and wires, leaving a significant gap in understanding
their seismic performance. Given the innovative use of SMA wires for enhancing seismic
safety in structures, it is essential to conduct comprehensive studies on their behavior under
various cyclic and earthquake loading conditions. The present study aims to evaluate the
seismic behavior of SMA ropes with different layouts based on both computer simulations
and experimental investigations. This study aims to comprehensively investigate and
compare the dynamic performance of steel and SMA ropes with different configurations
using finite element (FE) analysis and shaking table modeling. To this end, the commercial
SMA rope’s behavior is simulated in ABAQUS [23], and the simulation is verified by
reference to the experimentally evaluated behavior. Subsequently, different rope layouts
are examined under earthquake excitation and quasi-static sinusoidal loading protocols.
To validate the simulations, shaking table tests are performed on full-scale steel ropes,
enabling a comparative analysis of the behaviors exhibited by SMA and steel ropes.

blocks.text:
A wire rope is a composite structure composed of twisted steel wires, organized into
strands and wound around a core. These wires are drawn to precise dimensions and
intertwined in specific configurations to form each strand. Subsequently, the required
number of strands is helically wrapped around the core, which may consist of various
materials such as synthetic or natural fibers, metallic strands, or an independent wire rope
core (refer to Figure 1). In this study, the rope’s wire size, number, arrangement, strand
count, lay, and core type were determined based on prior research [14,24,25].

In Figure 1, cross-section schematics depicting the various components of the wire rope
are provided. The first rope features wires with a diameter of 1 mm. An identifier ‘A × B’
was designated for the other five types of ropes, where ‘A’ represents the number of strands
and ‘B’ signifies the number of wires in each strand. For example, 1 × 3, 1 × 7, 1 × 19,
and 1 × 27 ropes were derived from a single strand comprising 3, 7, 19, and 27 wires,
respectively. The 1 × 3 rope was a unilayer cable lacking a core, while all other ropes
consisted of single or multi-layered constructions with an inner core. The 7 × 7 rope (left
regular lay) comprised 7 strands, with each strand containing 7 wires, each with a diameter
of 1 mm. Additionally, it was assumed that one of the ropes with a 1 × 7 configuration was
a bundle.

blocks.text:
In this study, an experiment was undertaken in which a steel structural system was
positioned on the shake table at the Laboratory of Structural Earthquake Engineering
(SEE-Lab) at the University of Bonab, located in the East Azerbaijan province of Iran. The
shake table is a product of SANTAM engineering design company [27] and the tests on
the ropes within the steel structural system included both cyclic loading and simulated
earthquake excitations.

The primary objective is to design a structural configuration capable of withstanding
the tensile forces exerted by the embedded ropes during seismic events. The design process
focuses on identifying the rope that generates the highest force within the structure, thereby
necessitating the consideration of tension forces for that specific rope only. In this context,
the 7 × 7 rope emerges as the critical element responsible for producing the maximum force
within the system. An overview representation of the experimental setup is depicted in
Figure 4. This figure provides a zoomed-in view of the middle section of the device shown
in Figure 5, enabling a closer observation of the central part of the setup.

distributed among the cross-sectional areas. It should be noted that due to unintentional
reasons encountered during the data acquisition process, some of the data were missing,
resulting in the inability to plot the complete cycle in Figure 8g.

The instability or fluctuations observed in the cyclic loading curve of the steel wire
ropes during the loading phase can be attributed to a combination of different factors.
Frictional effects between the individual twisted wires, the nonlinear behavior of the steel
material, geometric nonlinearities arising from changes in the rope structure, manufacturing
imperfections, and dynamic effects induced by the cyclic loading can all contribute to the
observed instability. Those complex factors, acting individually or in tandem, lead to the
fluctuations in the loading response.

lines.text: 2.2. Numerical Assessment

blocks.text:
In this section, the ABAQUS FE software [23] was utilized to simulate the behavior
of ropes under sinusoidal and seismic longitudinal displacements. Initially, the ropes
were designed in SolidWorks using specifications from laboratory experiments and then
imported into ABAQUS. The material properties of the steel ropes were defined based on
real stress–strain values obtained from tensile testing, while plastic stress–strain values
from Table 3 were used for the simulations. Superelastic properties were assigned to SMA
materials according to Table 3. The FE modeling employed a hexagonal element shape with
a constant mesh size of 2 mm, following Biggs [25] as a reference (see Figure 9). Figure 9
illustrates the schematic of the rope and the loading setup.

blocks.text:
The ropes were modeled using C3D8R solid elements, which are eight-node hexa-
hedral elements with hourglass control. The “Surface-to-Surface” contact algorithm was
used to simulate the actual contact between the wires in the wire rope. The penalty friction
algorithm was applied to model the tangential frictional behavior between the lateral
surfaces of the individual wires, and the friction coefficient was set to be 0.5. The normal
behavior between the wires was defined as a hard contact [25,28]. As shown in Figure 9c,
reference points RP1 and RP2 were defined at the center of each end surface of the rope
core. The corresponding nodes on each end surface of the wire rope were coupled with
RP1 and RP2. All the degrees of freedom of RP2 were constrained, while reference point
1 was allowed to move solely along the rope’s longitudinal axis.
The loading process in the FE model was simulated using the dynamic explicit method,
incorporating two types of loads: sinusoidal (0.01 Hz) and seismic excitation (El Centro scaled
earthquake) applied to reference point 1. The loading was displacement-controlled, with 8 mm
displacements for the SMA and 11 mm for the steel rope. Sinusoidal loading’s cyclic nature
enables the simulation of real vibrations and motions induced by earthquakes, machinery,
transportation, and wind effects. The details of the considered earthquake are presented
in Table 4 and Figure 10, sourced from the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center

curve indicates that the behavior of all the various rope arrangements is almost similar,
with any slight differences attributed to the twisting angle of the ropes.

In Biggs’s study [25], SMA cables with varying helix angles of 10◦, 17◦, and 21◦were

simultaneously reducing cable stress levels.
