3.1. Behavior of SMA Ropes under Sinusoidal Load

blocks.text:
In Figure 17, the response of the SMA under sinusoidal loading with a frequency of
0.01 Hz is shown as a force versus displacement curve. The findings indicate a nearly linear
relationship between the tensile force of ropes and the number of wires comprising them,
where the force exerted by the rope is equivalent to the summation of the forces exerted
by its individual wires. As illustrated in Figure 17a, the force corresponding to maximum
displacement (8 mm) is approximately 365 N for one SMA wire; this translates to about
1.09, 2.40, 6.01, 8.1, and 14 kN, respectively for 1 × 3, 1 × 7, 1 × 19, 1 × 27, and 7 × 7 SMA
ropes. It can be inferred that the tensile efficiency of the rope decreases with an increase in
the number of wires.

lines.text: 3.3. Study on SMA Rope Behavior Sensitivity to Cable Arrangement

blocks.text:
The stress–strain behavior of SMA ropes under the El Centro earthquake scenario has
been investigated using the FE method. In this regard, Figure 19 presents a comparison
of the stress–strain responses of various SMA rope configurations, including wire, 1 × 3,
1 × 7, 1 × 7 bundle, 1 × 19, 1 × 27, and 7 × 7 ropes with helix angles of 0, 3, 5, 7, 9, and
13 degrees, respectively. It is noteworthy that all investigated ropes exhibit superelastic
behavior; however, their mechanical responses vary slightly. For instance, the 7 × 7 rope
demonstrates a smaller loading plateau stress and a larger plateau strain compared to the
other ropes. This observation suggests that increasing the helix angle of the ropes leads
to a decrease in stress and an increase in strain. Nonetheless, in general, their mechanical
behavior is similar to that of a single wire.

blocks.text: 4. Conclusions

lines.text: 4. Conclusions

blocks.text:
In this study, the mechanical behaviors of helically symmetric laboratory-fabricated
SMA and steel wire ropes when subjected to earthquake excitation and quasi-static sinu-
soidal loading protocols are explored. Both experimental and numerical methodologies are
employed to investigate their responses. The conclusions drawn are listed as follows:
•
The findings indicated a good agreement between numerical calculations and labora-
tory outcomes for SMA ropes, suggesting FE simulation as a reliable tool for prelimi-
nary assessments. Consequently, it is anticipated that the seismic response of SMA
wires, akin to their steel counterparts, is somewhat influenced by wire configurations
but largely retains the superelastic attributes akin to a single wire.
•

pure tension loading are similar. Additionally, under quasi-static sinusoidal loading

There’s a near-linear relationship between SMA rope tensile force and the number of

The SMA 1 × 3 and 1 × 7 ropes exhibit seismic responses akin to those observed
under sinusoidal loading conditions, particularly concerning maximum force. This
observation underscores the potential of SMA ropes as a promising material for
applications demanding high strength and resilience under seismic loading.
Under the El Centro earthquake scenario, increasing the helix angle in SMA ropes
reduces stress and increases strain, while their overall behavior resembles that of a
single wire. However, further investigations under diverse seismic excitations are
recommended to enhance our understanding of their performance.

blocks.text:
This study of the mechanical behavior of helically symmetric SMA and steel wire
ropes under earthquake and quasi-static sinusoidal loading has yielded valuable insights,
but several opportunities for further research remain to expand the scope and depth of
the investigation. Exploring a broader range of rope configurations, conducting dynamic
testing with realistic seismic excitations, investigating the influence of design parameters
and evaluating durability, and comparing the performance of steel wire and SMA ropes
under the same seismic conditions as well as assessing their feasibility and performance
in real-world structures could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the ropes’
behavior and their potential applications in seismic-resistant structures.

In the past decades, the robotics community has made great progress in the development of soft robots that are 
inherently safe in their interaction with their environment. However, the compliance of these robots also comes 
with drawbacks, such as the fact that soft structures cannot easily exert high forces on their environment. In this 
work, we propose a new soft actuator where part of the structure can actively switch from being compliant to 
rigid by using particle jamming in some sections. A challenge with jamming particle designs is that it requires a 
vacuum pump which tends to be bulky, which we have addressed here by directly embedding a flexible electro- 
conjugated fluid (ECF) micropump in the actuator. This bidirectional pump does not affect the flexibility of the 
soft actuator, but when it is switched on, pressures up to ± 55 kPa are achieved. We demonstrate that these 
embedded pumps can be used both to increase the stiffness of the actuator with a factor of 5.5 by an ECF pressure 
of −55 kPa as well as to inflate the actuator and achieve hydraulic actuation with a bending angle of 16◦by + 55 
kPa. We believe that the proposed soft actuator that can actively switch stiffness and produce deformation is an 
important tool for the development of more practical soft robots.

creatures to survive [1]. Interestingly, living creatures require both 
gentle interaction with their surroundings when they are, for instance, 
feeding youngsters or playing instruments, while at the same time, high 
force interactions are needed when building nests or hunting [2]. The 
marvel of both the dexterity and adaptability of our bodies’ stiffness to 
carry out various tasks is the result of many factors, including the bone 
and joint structure combined with antagonistic muscle pairs, which 
allow to firm up parts of our bodies or relax them [3]. The ability to 
control the stiffness of bodies is even observed in invertebrates such as 
octopuses that can vary the stiffness of their arms, allowing them to 
interact with the surrounding water dynamically [4]. This also allows 
them to create virtual joints leading to a virtually unlimited number of 
degrees of freedom in their arm movements [5]. So far, the fields of 
conventional stiff robotics and the upcoming soft robotics community

blocks.text:
Variable stiffness robots have the on-demand ability to change their 
stiffness between rigid state and compliant state depending on the task 
they are carrying out [20,21], in essence, this mimics strategies used by 
living creatures such as octopuses’ tentacles and elephants’ trunks [22]. 
Different strategies have been developed to create materials that mimic 
these properties [23] which can be categorized in semi-active materials 
and active materials [24]. Semi-active materials, including shape 
memory alloys (SMAs) [25], shape memory polymers (SMPs) [26], 
low-melting-point alloys (LMPAs) [27], granular materials [28], change 
their microscopic structure upon the stimulation of external energy, 
affecting their mechanical properties. In contrast, active materials such 
as piezoelectric polymers (PZPs) [29], ferromagnetic shape memory 
alloys (FSMAs) [30] convert the energy form and use this energy to 
modulate the mechanical properties.

blocks.text:
Although the robotic community has developed many variable 
stiffness robots based on these materials, many remaining limitations 
prevent these robots from being applied to practical situations. For 
example, thermoplastic materials like SMPs, non-SMPs, and LMPAs 
demonstrate a wide range of working stiffness (0.1 ~ 10 MPa), but the 
response time is slow (approximately 100 s) [31–36]. In contrast, 
granular materials have a faster response time (about 1 s) with a similar 
range of working stiffness (2 ~ 100 MPa) [37–39], so that it will be a 
promising solution for the current issue of robotics.

blocks.text:
Among many technologies for stiffness control in robotics, the 
granular jamming transition has been attractive because it is simple, 
versatile, reversible, and customizable for specific applications [40]. 
Granular materials change the stiffness based on the jamming phe­
nomenon in which the stiffness of the materials varies according to the 
vacuum pressure applied to them. A granular jamming actuator con­
sisted of an elastic envelope filled with granular material [41]. At at­
mospheric pressure, the particles within the envelope are at a fluid-liked 
state. However, when the air evacuates from the envelope, the particles 
change from the fluid-liked state to the rigid-liked state, increasing the 
stiffness of the system [42]. Employing this phenomenon, Brown et al. 
[43] introduced a universal gripper attached to a conventional robot 
arm as an end-effector. The gripper consisted of an elastic sphere bag 
filled with ground coffee. At a fluid-liked state, the gripper pressed the 
target object and adapted to the shape and the object. When vacuum 
pressure was applied, the gripper changed to a rigid-like state and 
maintained adequate force to grasp the object. Pei Jiang et al. [44] 
introduced a soft actuator integrated with the granular jamming module 
in another application of various stiffness actuation. The device con­
sisted of a fibre reinforcement soft actuator at the upper part and a bag of 
granular materials at the lower part. The authors pressurized the two 
chambers separately, and the differential pressure between the two 
chambers determined the bending motion and the stiffness of the 
actuator.

compressor, a vacuum pump, and many control units such as valves with 
clunky tubing for its manipulation. To overcome these limitations, we 
focus on a functional fluid, electro-conjugate fluid (ECF). By using the 
dynamic pumping mechanism of the ECF (a kind of dielectric fluid) 
converting electric energy directly into kinetic energy [45–47], we can 
realize an ECF micropump composed of the triangular prism and slit 
electrode pairs (TPSEs), as shown in Fig. 1, which can be embedded in 
the miniaturized robot as a micro hydraulic power source [48–50]. Since 
its components such as the TPSEs and the microchannels are fabricated 
by photolithography-based MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) 
technology [51,52], this micropump is superior in integrability with 
other microfluidic device elements[53–55]. By taking advantage of high 
output power density [56,57], we have applied the ECF micropumps to 
various soft robots [58,59]. In addition, the soft actuator driven by ECF 
flow has good repeatability and reliability, as demonstrated in a robot 
hand [60], in which five independent robot fingers (soft actuators) have 
almost identical performance at room temperature. We also demon­
strated that our ECF micropumps could activate the jamming transition 
in the jamming gripper if we adopt proper particles [61,62].

Based on the background mentioned above, this paper proposes a 
new miniaturized soft actuator with switchable stiffness using a granular 
jamming system activated by an embedded ECF micropump as a micro 
hydraulic power source. In addition to the advanced feature of the in­
ternal pressure source, the proposed soft actuator has the advantage of 
two functions in the same body: (1) changing its stiffness based on 
granular jamming by negative pressure of ECF jet flow and (2) actuating 
(bending motion) by its positive pressure, as shown in Fig. 2. This paper 
is organized as follows: the concept and working principle of the pro­
posed soft actuator are described in Section 2. The fabrication and the 
characteristic evaluation are covered in Section 3 and Section 4, 
respectively. Finally, the conclusions of the research are given in Section 
5.

The proposed soft actuator consists of two main parts: (1) the soft 
actuator filled with jamming particles (aluminium oxide, 20 µm in 
diameter) and (2) the bidirectional flexible ECF micropump. Fig. 3 de­
scribes the schematics and dimensions of the soft actuator. We adopt a 
Pneu-Nets soft actuator as the structure of our device [64]. The Pneu-Net 
soft actuator contains a series of channels and chambers made of a soft 
material (SYLGARD™ 184, Dow Inc.). Inside the channels and the 
chambers, we fill the aluminium oxide particles with a diameter of 
20 µm to serve the two-functional purpose of the device. Below this soft 
actuator, we integrate the bidirectional ECF micropump. The ECF 
micropump here contains tiny triangular prism and slit electrode pairs 
(TPSEs) on a thin polyimide substrate so that the micropump is not 
stretchable but flexible. This flexible micropump can work as a 
displacement constraint element and bend upon the actuation of the 
upper part. The micropump and the soft actuator connect through the 
small port covered by the filter made of a metallic mesh. The filter 
prevents the particles inside the soft actuator from flowing into the 
channel of the micropump, protecting the micropump when it works at 
high voltage. We describe details of the dimensions in Fig. 3. We sub­
stitute the rhombic prism for the triangular prism of the TPSEs to pro­
vide the flow in two directions for the micropump, ensuring the 
micropump can replace the air compressor and the vacuum pump. The 
essential dimensions of the electrodes are based on the optimal TPSE 
dimensions reported in our previous study [57]: (a) Electrode gap 
(distance between the sharp tip of the rhombic prism to the slit elec­
trode) is 0.2 mm; (b) Slit width (distance between two rectangular 
prisms in the slit electrode) is 0.2 mm; and Slit depth (thickness of the 
split electrodes) is 0.3 mm. Concerning the wiring, the red electrodes 
connect to the high voltage and the blue electrodes connect to the

blocks.text: 3.1. Fabrication of the soft actuator

lines.text: 3.1. Fabrication of the soft actuator

blocks.text:
Fig. 4 describes the details of the casting process of the soft actuator 
filled with jamming particles. We used the casting method to fabricate 
the soft actuator. In the first step, we prepared the casting moulds by 
machining the polyetherimide into the mould shapes. The moulds had 
two parts inserted into each other to form the shape of the Pneu-Nets 
actuator. Fig. 5a shows the optical image of the moulds used to cast 
the soft actuator. In casting steps, we first mixed silicone elastomer 
(SYLGARD™ 184, Dow Inc.) with its curing agent in the ratio of 10:1. 
Next, we removed air bubbles from the silicone elastomer mixture in the

blocks.text: 3.2. Fabrication of the bidirectional flexible ECF micropump

lines.text: 3.2. Fabrication of the bidirectional flexible ECF micropump

blocks.text:
We basically have utilized glass substrates to fabricate bidirectional 
ECF micropumps [63]. However, in the proposed soft actuator with 
switchable stiffness, we need the flexibility of the micropump. There­
fore, we fabricate the micropump on a commercial polyimide flexible 
printed circuit board, called as FPCB (NZ-M1K, Sunhayato Co. Ltd.). The 
FPCB consists of five layers: reinforcing plate (thickness: 1 mm), adhe­
sive layer (thickness: 20 µm), polyimide (PI) layer (thickness: 50 µm), 
copper layer (thickness: 35 µm) and positive photoresist layer (thick­
ness: several µm). The reinforcing plate bind to the polyimide layer due 
to the function of the mediate adhesive layer. The reinforcing plate 
provides a robust substrate to ensure ease in handling the thin and soft PI 
film during fabricating steps. After fabrication, the reinforcing plate is 
detached from the PI layer by dipping the whole FPCB inside the ethanol 
for an adequate time.

After fabricating the upper soft actuator and the lower flexible ECF 
micropump, we combined these two components to realize the proposed 
soft actuator with switchable stiffness using a micropump-activated 
jamming system. First, we used a punch to make the port to the bot­
tom sheet of the soft actuator and the upper cover of the sealed micro­

sheet to serve as a filter to prevent the aluminium oxide particles from

blocks.text:
We cannot measure the output pressure and flow rate of the fabri­
cated micropump in our assembled soft actuator due to the integrated 
design of the device, although understanding the pressure and flow rate 
according to the applied voltage is essential to evaluate the performance 
of the proposed soft actuator. Therefore, we measured the output pres­
sure under the no-flow condition and the flow rate under the no-load 
condition by the experimental setup shown in Fig. 9. First, we con­
nected the device to the pressure sensor and applied high voltage to the 
micropump to measure the pressure. Next, we measured the mass of a 
breaker below the output port and time to calculate the flow rate of the 
ECF micropump. In both experiments, we applied the voltage to the 
micropump from 0 to 2.5 kV with an increment of 0.5 kV.

blocks.text:
The sealed micropump consisted of TPSEs on the flexible substrate 
and the PDMS channel (3 mm in thickness), which was utilized for the 
only evaluation of the micropump. The size of the micropump was 24 
(length) × 8 (width) × 3 (height) mm in total. In one flow direction, the 
micropump contained three electrode pairs in parallel and 27 electrodes 
pairs in series. Because the micropump worked based on the ECF effect, 
we could control the flow rate or the pressure by changing the voltage 
applied to the micropump. As shown in Fig. 10, the output pressure and 
the flow rate increased according to the increase of the applied voltage. 
We recorded the maximum pressure of 55 kPa flow rate of 140 mm3/s at 
the applied voltage of 2.5 kV. The result proves that we can use our 
micropump in soft robot applications where space is limited. The other 
advantage of our micropump is that it can generate the flow in two di­
rections. We found that the flow generated from left to right was higher 
than one in the opposite direction. However, the difference was not 
noticeable, 11% for the static pressure and 3% for the flow rate. We 
believed that the difference in the pressure was higher than the differ­
ence in the flow rate, which resulted from the expansion of the PDMS 
channel due to fabrication error. During the characterization of the

We showed the experimental results of the changing stiffness ex­
periments in Fig. 11b. When we did not apply voltage to the ECF 
micropump, the soft actuator was at its initial state. When we applied 
the negative pressure to the soft actuator, the jamming phenomenon 
affected its stiffness. When the negative pressure increased, the bending 
force increased. Initially, the bending force of the soft actuator at 3 mm 
was 0.134 N. When we applied −50 kPa to the soft actuator, the 
bending force at 3 mm was 0.743 N, showing an increment of 5.5 times 
compared to its initial state. This proved that our ECF micropump could 
actuate the jamming effect and switch the stiffness of the device as 
needed.

We also demonstrated that our actuator could carry the load 5.2 
times larger than its weight (Fig. 12). In this experiment, we first applied 
2.5 kV to the micropump to generate a negative pressure inside the 
actuator. Then we placed a mass of 130 g on the tip of the soft actuator 
whose weight is 25 g. The actuator could carry the mass as long as the 
applied voltage remained. When we turned the applied voltage off, the 
mass felt from the tip of the soft actuator.

blocks.text:
In this experiment, the stiffness of our soft actuator was increased 
when negative pressure was generated for the granular jamming by 
applying the voltage to the flexible ECF micropump. Therefore, the 
stiffened soft actuator could carry the load much larger than its weight. 
However, the stiffness of the soft actuator returned to its initial softness 
by turning off the voltage supply, causing the mass to fall off from its tip. 
This result showed that the original stiffness of the soft actuator was not 
strong enough to tolerate a similar load. In other words, the switchable 
stiffness function of our device improved the load-bearing of the soft 
actuator.

blocks.text: 5. Conclusion

lines.text: 5. Conclusion

blocks.text:
In this article, we introduced a novel soft actuator that can actively 
adjust the stiffness by controlling the voltage applied to its internal 
micropump to induce a jammed state of granular materials in the soft 
actuator. We also solved the long-standing challenge of the jamming 
particle designs and the soft robots, which are the bulky vacuum pump 
and air compressor. We directly integrated a flexible electro-conjugated 
fluid (ECF) micropump in the soft actuator. This bidirectional pump had 
the function of the vacuum pump and applied up to −50 kPa to the soft 
actuator for an increase of 5.5 times in stiffness. Moreover, when we 
switched the flow of this bidirectional pump, it had the same function as 
the air compressor and applied up to + 50 kPa to the soft actuator to 
realize the bending movement of 16◦. We believe that the reported soft 
actuator that can actively switch stiffness and actuation is a promising 
solution for developing more practical soft robots.

actuator. We also solved the long-standing challenge of the jamming
particle designs and the soft robots, which are the bulky vacuum pump
and air compressor. We directly integrated a flexible electro-conjugated
fluid (ECF) micropump in the soft actuator. This bidirectional pump had
the function of the vacuum pump and applied up to −50 kPa to the soft
actuator for an increase of 5.5 times in stiffness. Moreover, when we
switched the flow of this bidirectional pump, it had the same function as
the air compressor and applied up to + 50 kPa to the soft actuator to
realize the bending movement of 16◦. We believe that the reported soft
actuator that can actively switch stiffness and actuation is a promising
solution for developing more practical soft robots.

blocks.text:
Huy Hoang Huynh received the bachelor degree in Mechatronics from Ho Chi Minh City 
University of Technology, Vietnam in 2016 and received the degree of Master of Engi­
neering in Mechanical Engineering from Tokyo Institute of Technology in 2018. He is 
currently a Ph.D. candidate in Mechanical Engineering at Tokyo Institute of Technology 
from September 2018. Since he joined Tokyo Institute of Technology, he has developed 
technical expertise in Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS). His research includes 
the development of micropumps and its applications to cooling systems and soft robotics.

blocks.text:
Dong Han received the B.E. from Xi’an Jiaotong University (XJTU), China, in 2011, and 
the M.E. degree from Zhejiang University (ZJU), China, in 2014. Then he received the M.E. 
and Dr. Eng. Degrees from Tokyo Institute of Technology (Tokyo Tech), Japan, in 2016, 
and 2018, respectively. From 2018–2020, he worked as an Assistant Professor at the 
Laboratory for Future Interdisciplinary Research of Science and Technology (FIRST), 
Tokyo Tech. He has been a doctoral supervisor at State Key Laboratory of Fluid Power and 
Mechatronic Systems and School of Mechanical Engineering, Zhejiang University. His 
current research interests include microfluidics, microrobots, electromagnetic actuators 
and sensors, energy harvesters, micro motors.

blocks.text:
Kazuhiro Yoshida received the B.E. degree in electrical engineering from Yokohama 
National University, Japan in 1984 and the M.E. and Ph.D. degrees in control engineering 
from Tokyo Institute of Technology, Japan in 1986 and 1989, respectively. After working 
as a research associate, an associate professor, and a professor at Precision and Intelligence 
Laboratory, he is now a professor at FIRST, IIR, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Japan. His 
research interests include microactuators, power microrobots, and functional fluids ap­
plications. He is a member of the Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers, the Japan Fluid 
Power System Society, IEEE, and similar associations.

blocks.text:
Michael De Volder performed his Ph.D. research on MEMS actuators at the KU Leuven in 
Belgium and in part at the Tokyo Institute of Technology in Japan. During his postdoc, he 
worked on nanotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of 
Michigan, Harvard University, KU Leuven, and Imec. In 2013, he joined the Department of 
Engineering at the University of Cambridge where he holds a professorship in Advanced 
Materials Engineering. His work currently focuses on energy storage devices and nano­
technology scale-up.

blocks.text:
Joon-Wan Kim received his degree of Bachelor of Science from the department of Me­
chanical Engineering at the POSTECH in 1999. He received his degree of Master of Science 
and Ph.D. at the Department of Precision Engineering, Graduate School of Engineering, the 
University of Tokyo in 2005. From 2002–2005, he was also a Junior Research Associate at 
Materials Fabrication Laboratory, RIKEN. He was an assistant professor from 2005 to 2013 
in Tokyo Institute of Technology. He has been an Associate Professor in the Institute of 
Innovative Research (IIR), Tokyo Institute of Technology. His current interests are 
micromachining and MEMS for functional fluid devices.
